translation:
LXI.

DELPHINIUM                    DELPHINIUM, THE OTHER

Some call it diachyton, others diachysis, others paralysis, others kammaros, others hyacinth, others hyphidion, others aras, others delpheinias, others nerion, others epreiadion, others sosandron, others kronion; the Romans call it bucinus minor. It sends up straight shoots from a single root, a cubit long or even longer, bearing numerous small leaves that are deeply divided, dolphin-shaped — whence it also got its name. It bears seed in pods, resembling millet. The seed of this plant, taken as a drink with wine, helps those stung by scorpions as no other remedy does. They also say that if the herb is placed near scorpions it paralyzes them, making them inactive and numb, and that when it is taken away they return to their former state. It grows in rough and sunny places.

Some call it hyacinth; the Romans call it bucinus. This one too resembles the one described before it, but its leaves and stems are much more slender. It has the same power as the one previously mentioned, though it is not as effective.

[marginalia: "delphinium" / "delphinium, the other"]

translation:
LXII.

DITTANY                              ANOTHER DITTANY

Dittany: some call it belonakos, some
call it artemidion, some Cretan [herb], some
call it ephemeron, some bladia, some belitokos,
some dorkidion, some elbounion;
the Romans [call it] ustilago rustica; some
call it the pennyroyal of Ariadne.
In the city of the Bactrians there is
a mountain-herb like the Cretan [dittany],
similar to pennyroyal in its leaves, but larger and woolly,
and it has certain bristly growths on its
leaves; it bears neither flower nor fruit.
It does the same things as the cultivated pennyroyal,
but much more effectively — not merely
when drunk, but also when applied as a plaster or
fumigated, it shakes loose even deeply embedded
splinters, they say. And it is said that goats in Crete,
when wounded by arrows, having grazed on this plant
straightaway expel the arrows.

[Another Dittany]
Some call it ephemeron, some
bladia; the Romans [call it] ustilago.
It grows in Crete, and there is another
kind of dittany, similar to this one
in its leaves, but smaller; its
flower, however, is larger
[and] of similar appearance,
as is customary for soft [plants];
and the smell of its leaf,
along with its pungency, is
marsh-like and snail-shell-shaped [?].
It does [things] in a similar way
to that one, that is, being
present, it is mixed [into remedies]
and applied in plasters as well.

translation: ...the roots, when ground up with honey and applied as a plaster, heal malignant ulcers and spreading sores, especially when combined with white vine (bryony); and mixed with honey they close up fistulas when applied, and they bring about the destruction of embryos. Applied with honey they also cure skin blemishes (alphos), while the "octopus-like" growths (polyps) and cancerous growths they consume away. The juice of the root is also useful for the eyes, against cloudiness, white opacities, and dimness of vision. The smell of the root and of the freshly gathered herb causes miscarriage. Thirty seeds of its fruit, drunk with vinegar-water, are given [for this purpose]; some give them with the juice of the plant itself. They also use it as an eyewash for those suffering eye pain, mixed with olive oil. The leaves, being astringent, are applied to fresh wounds. When steeped in wine they are given to those who have dysentery. It is also said that those who rub their hands with it, or handle the root, are not bitten by snakes.

SMALL DRACONTEA (Dragon Arum)          LAUREL (Daphne)                    DAPHNOIDES

Some call it aron, some aris, some
eparsis, some parnogon,
some kynosbolon, some phoinikeon,
some onokephalon,
some ephialtion; the Egyptians call it
ebron; the Romans call it erythmon;
the Thuscans call it betaleporina;
the Istrians call it gigaroum; the
Dacians call it dagma; their own
word is nekoum; the Africans call it
aterni; the Syrians call it chlam
loufan. It has leaves similar to
those of the dracontium, aspilota
(spotless), a stem about a span long,
somewhat reddish, wing-like; above
it the fruit is saffron-colored; it has
a white root like that of the dracontium,
which is both cooked and eaten,
being pungent. Its seed has
the same power as its leaves and root,
as said above for the dracontium.
The root, when ground together with
bulbs, is applied as a plaster for
gout sufferers, because it is not as
smooth and black [as that of dracontium],
but it is more edible.

Some call it the Alexandrian [laurel], some call it idea,
some call it Danae, some zalia,
some stephane, some Daphne of
Samothrace, some mithrios,
some hypoglossion.
It has leaves like those of myrtle-box,
but larger and softer
and lighter in color; its fruit
is in the middle of the leaves, reddish,
about the size of a chickpea, and
larger than that of the myrtle-box; its root
grows near the surface of the earth and
is harsh; it grows in similar places
as the myrtle-box, being milder
and more fragrant, growing in straight,
upright places. Its power is this:
when its root is drunk, it brings on the flow
of menses; together with sweet wine
it helps women suffering difficult
childbirth, and relieves bladder
discomfort. Also helps in cases of
chills.

Some call it eupetalon, some
daphnoeides, some chamaidaphne,
some call it hypepilon.
It is a shrub about a cubit high
with many branches, having leaves
near the top, leaf-bearing,
with bark around its branches
that is somewhat sticky; its leaves
are strong, resembling those
of laurel but softer
and stronger; they do not
burn or bite the mouth when chewed.
Its flowers are white, its fruit
black when ripe.

translation:
LXX.

EUZOMON (Rocket)

The Romans call it eruca, the Egyptians threkekikin, the Africans assourek. Eaten in excess, it stirs sexual desire, and its seed is diuretic and aids digestion. They use the seed as a seasoning for cooked dishes, and they also preserve it to keep for a long time by kneading it with vinegar or with milk and forming it into little cakes.

ERYSIMON (Hedge Mustard)

Some call it chamaiplion, the prophets call it herakleous, the Egyptians call it alphita, the Romans ergomon or erionem. It grows around cities, on building plots, and in gardens. Its leaves resemble those of wild rocket, somewhat narrower, and its flowers are yellowish at the tip. At the end it has slender, curved, horn-shaped pods containing seed a little like cress or turnip seed, similar also in taste. It helps against inflammations of the face and against catarrh, coughs, jaundice, and sciatica, when licked up with honey. Drunk, it helps against deadly poisons. Applied as a plaster with water, it helps hidden tumors, hard swellings of the breasts, parotid swellings, and inflammations of the glands. It has a thinning effect and generally warms the body. It becomes gentler for treating the blood when soaked in water and boiled, and then eaten with fat, having been roasted and ground into a paste.

ELELISPHAKON (SAGE)

Some call it elelisphakon, some phakon,
some konin, some sphagnos, some
bekion; the Egyptians call it apousi; the Romans
call it salvia; some call it korsalon.
It is a tall, many-branched shrub
having four-sided, somewhat whitish
stems, and leaves resembling
quince leaves, but longer and
rougher, whitish-downy, like
the nap rubbed up on cloaks,
fragrant. It bears its fruit at
the tips of its stalks, like
wild clary. It grows in
rough places. The decoction
of its branches and leaves,
when drunk, promotes urine,
blackens the hair, and
closes wounds; it is good for
cleansing malignant ulcers.
The decoction of it, mixed with
wine and used as a douche, stops
itching around the genitals; and its
leaves, boiled in wine and
drunk, stop bleeding.

EPHEMERON (MEADOW SAFFRON)

Some call it kolchikon, some
boulbon agrion; the Romans
call it "bulbus agrestis."
It flowers at the end of autumn,
with a whitish flower similar to crocus;
afterward it bears leaves similar
to those of the bulb, but broader,
and a stem about a span long,
having a tawny-black color;
its root, when boiled, is
soft and tender, found to be
sweet in the middle. The bulb
has a single growth in the middle,
from which it sends up its flower.
It grows mostly in Messenia
and in Colchis. If eaten, it kills
by suffocation, like the poppy.
I have described it so that no
one unknowingly mistake it for
a true bulb, for it is deceptive
and causes unexpected harm
through the pain it brings. It is
more quickly helped by things
like mushrooms and other such
things, taken as a drink, than by
anything else needing
further remedy.

HELLEBORINE                          WHITE HELLEBORE

Some call it epipaktis, some call it     Some call it askeda, some call it ektomon, some
borion. It is a small shrub with very    call it pnagataxaris; prophets [call it] the offspring
tiny leaves; it is drunk against every   of Heracles; some call it polyidos, some call it
deadly poison and against liver          anaphystos; the Egyptians [call it] somphia; some
ailments.                                call it ounre; the Romans [call it] veletrumal;
                                          the Gauls [call it] lagonon; some call it anesta.
                                          Its leaves are similar to those of plantain
                                          (arnoglossos), but shorter, and with a red rib; it
                                          [must] be dried. It has many thin roots growing
                                          from a small head, like an onion.

It grows in mountainous places. The roots must be dug up around the time of the grape harvest. The best kind is the one of moderate size, white, and fleshy inside, dry, hollow, and sharp/pungent to the taste. The finest is the Antikyrian kind, then the Galatian and Cappadocian, which is more rush-like and more suffocating [in effect]. It purges through vomiting in various ways. It is also mixed into eye salves that are able to clear away dimness affecting the pupils. It induces menstruation and, if applied, kills the embryo. It also provokes sneezing and kills mice when mixed with honey and barley meal and offered to them, dissolving them. It is given for other purposes too, mixed with thapsia juice, coarse meal, and honey-water, or in a lentil broth, made into bread or pellets. It has also been elaborately treated, more so than any other subject, by those who have written before about its proper dosage—most of all by Philo of Cos, who did not wish to record a therapeutic regimen for giving it. Some give it together with a decoction drink, or with coarse meal, offering only a small amount of food beforehand.

It is called melampodion because it is said that
a goatherd named Melampus was the first to purge
and heal the daughters of Proitos who had gone mad
with it. It has green leaves resembling... bears
a rather short stem, purple flowers shaped like roses;
it also has fruit like that of safflower, which the people
of Antikyra themselves call "sesame-like," using it
for purges. It has slender black roots that hang,
as it were, from a single onion-like head, from which
it is used. It grows in rough, dug-over ground and in
dry places. The best is that gathered from such regions,
such as the one from Antikyra; the finest black hellebore
grows there, with a firm, well-nourished white pith,
sharp to the taste and fiery. Such also is the hellebore
of Helikon and Parnassos, though the Helikonian kind
differs somewhat. It purges the upper bowel, drawing
off phlegm and bile, taken by itself or with scammony,
and a drachma of salt...

ERINEOS, also called eris,
also thryas, also polyrrhizon;
the Romans call it ouindikta.
The stem is not large, resembling ivy,
bearing eleven or ten leaves.
It produces neither fruit nor flower.
The roots are thin, black,
heavy-smelling, and foolish-tasting (bitter) when tasted.
It grows in moist places.
Its leaves, crushed and mixed with wine,
applied as a poultice to the breasts,
cause them to swell; it is an abortifacient.
Both the root and the leaves, crushed
and drunk in wine, continue the purgation
for five days.

Chapter 74.

HELXINE
Some call it helxitis, others kannabea,
others amelxine, others sougkrachos,
others [...]achou akanthos, others kistampelon,
others kissampethon, others
anatetamenon; the Romans call it
"vulos tulapalou," and the Egyptians
call it apal[...].
It has leaves similar to ivy, but smaller,
and a stem that is slender and twining,
wrapping itself around whatever is near.
Its shoots and tendrils are distinctive, and
it is used for bindings and wicker-work.
It has an astringent property, keeping
the bowels firm and the stomach [...]
settled.

EREINOS
Some call it okimoides, others hydri[...],
the Romans call it [...]timon; it is heard of
also as minorem; it grows beside rivers
and watery places, having leaves similar
to [...], mixed with [...] and standing
upright from below, with its upper
parts branching; it bears a flower
and a fruit that is dark in color, and
is full of a dense substance; its
petals [...], of these taken in the weight
of two drachms, mixed with a little
honey water and applied, checks
discharges from inflammations.
Drunk, it also stops looseness of the
bowels, and used as an ointment
with wine it is effective.

CHICKPEA (EREBINTHOS)

The Romans call it "cicer." It is diuretic, good for the bowels, promotes semen production, gives a good complexion, promotes the formation of kidney stones, brings on menstruation, and [helps expel] the embryo. It also increases the production of milk. It is applied as a poultice, especially when boiled together with bitter vetch, for inflammations, for ant-bite-like sores, and for scabies. However, for cancerous sores and malignant ulcers it is not suitable; [for these] barley and honey are applied as a poultice instead.

DODDER (EPITHYMON)

Some call it "kedris"; the Romans call it "gnuolucrum." It is the flower of a hard kind of thyme, resembling savory. Its heads are thin and light, having rough hairs. When finely prepared, it purges phlegm and black bile downward. It is suitable for melancholic patients who suffer from flatulence. Its decoction, drunk in a small dose of four drachms with honey, salt, and a little vinegar, is beneficial. It grows most abundantly in Pamphylia.

SMYRNION

It is also called hipposelinon; also agriolon; also "wild celery"; the Romans call it olus atrum. It is distinct from the other plant properly called "smyrnion," as we shall explain presently. It is larger and whiter than garden celery. The stem is hollow, tender, tall, as if marked with lines, having broader leaves, somewhat reddish, with foliage that whitens in the middle; at the flower-clusters it is three-forked and compact, the seed being black, somewhat elongated, coarse, and aromatic. The root is slender, fragrant, and pleasant to taste. It grows in shady places and in gardens, and it is eaten as a vegetable like celery — both leaves and stems, cooked or raw — and it is also prepared together with fish; by itself it is preserved in brine. Its fruit, when drunk with honeyed wine, induces menstruation; it warms those who are chilled when drunk, and when applied as an ointment it helps those suffering from strangury. The root, too, has the same effects when applied in the same way.

[marginal note]

flamula

ZOONYCHON

It is also called aetonychon; also leontopodion; also kemos; also ipheon; also katanankē; also damnamenē; also idiophyton; also phytobasion; also krossion; also krosophthalmon — the prophets (priests) call it "crocodile's blood"; also krokoperion among the Egyptians; the Laphnoines; the Romans call it Minervium; also neousmatos; also Palladium; also flammula.

It is a plant with "two-fingered" [small] leaves, having foliage about four fingers wide and three fingers long, rough and somewhat woolly near the root, and whitish beneath. At the top of the stems are heads as though cut off flat. Its fruit is hard to make out clearly because of the down that covers it. The flowers are of one color; the root is small, and they say it is very useful to physicians.

translation:
LXXVIII.

[Label: smooth smilax]
SMOOTH SMILAX

Its leaves are similar to ivy, but softer and smoother. Its stems, like those of the previous plant, have no thorns. It winds around trees just as the previous one does. It bears fruit like a necklace, small and black; above it has many white flowers all over the whole smilax plant, round and shady... In summer its leaves turn reddish like the date-palm's. When the fruit of this plant is drunk with wine, three Attic obols' weight of each, it is said to cause many troubled and disturbing dreams, as has been reported.

[Label: rough smilax]
ROUGH SMILAX

Some call it patetis, others call it lykanthemon, others agan eiketon, others heliophyton, others anatolikon, others lytikon, others blide, the Egyptians call it klyton, others aueide, the Romans call it konysson, mergina, others boulokroumlen..., others thyskoi radia. Its leaves are similar to those of honeysuckle, and its many thin shoots are thorny like the paliurus or the bramble. It winds around trees, spreading up and down, and bears fruit in the form of a cluster, like small leaflets, which ripen to a reddish-dark color, somewhat astringent to the taste; its root is hard and thick. It grows in marshy and rough places. The leaves and fruit of this plant are deadly; they are given beforehand or afterward as antidotes against poisons. It is said that if someone crushes some of it and gives it to a child to drink beforehand, the child will not be harmed by any venomous drug. It is also cut up for use in antidotes against poison.

ERIGERON

The Erechtheans and Romans call it "erigulus,"
others call it "senecio."
Its stem is about a span tall, somewhat reddish, with small leaves
deeply divided like those of rocket,
though much smaller, and flowers
that mature quickly, soon splitting open
and blossoming into what are called
"pappi" (downy tufts) — hence it is named
"erigeron" ("old man early," referring to the way
the round flower heads turn grey with age). Its root is
worthless. It grows especially
on walls and around cities.
Its property is astringent. The crushed
leaves, mixed with sweet wine,
or used alone, heal inflammations
of the testicles and fingers.
Mixed with frankincense, they heal other wounds
and treat fistulas.
The downy pappi, applied by themselves
as a poultice with vinegar, work similarly;
but if swallowed, the three
or four pappi can cause choking.

A dark blue variety is also found, with a shining black-tinted surface, which the physicians regard as of the finest sort.

HERAKLEION, OR PANKRATION                    HEMEROKALLES

Some also call this plant "skilla" (squill); but another kind of squill has a root like a bulb, somewhat purple, and fiery to the taste. Its leaves are like those of a lily, but longer. The root has the same power, preparation, and dosage as true squill, and it produces the same effects as the plants of that kind, though the power of this one is weaker than that of true squill. For this reason, when the root is pressed for its juice and mixed with bean-meal and formed into little loaves, it is given with honey-water, beneficially, to those suffering from spleen disease and dropsy.

Some call it "hemerokallis," others "krinon agrion" (wild lily), others "krinanthemon" (lily-flower), others "porphyranthes" (purple-flowered), others "bolbos emetikos" (vomiting bulb), and others "antikantharon." The Egyptians call it "iokry," the Romans "bubuli," and others "lilium marinum." It has leaves and stalks like the lily, but green like a leek. It bears flowers arranged along the stalk, three or four to a branch, resembling those of the lily, beginning to open wide at the tip. Its color is pale; its root resembles that of a bulb, of good size. When this root is dried and combined with honey and placed in wine, it acts as an expectorant and emmenagogue (it draws out phlegm and brings on menstruation). Its leaves, applied as a poultice, soothe inflammations of the breasts after childbirth and inflammations of the eyes. The root and leaves are also usefully applied as a poultice to burns.

GARDEN MINT                                    WILD MINT

Some call it "mintha," others "kalaminthe"; the Romans call it menta, others nepita; among the Egyptians it is called pherorumonthou, others perzo, others makio. It is a well-known plant, having a warming and drying power. Taken as a drink, its juice, mixed with vinegar, kills round worms; it stirs sexual desire, and stops hiccups, vomiting, and cholera when two or three sprigs are drunk with the juice of sour pomegranate. Applied as a poultice with barley meal, it disperses abscesses; placed on the forehead it relieves headache; it soothes swelling and pain of the breasts; it also helps when applied as a poultice to dog bites; its juice mixed with honey-water is good for earache. If placed in a woman before intercourse, it prevents conception; rubbed on a rough tongue, it smooths it; placed in milk, it keeps it from curdling; and it is a pleasant drink for inducing menstruation.

The Romans call the wild mint "mentastrum." It grows with hairier leaves and is in every way larger than the sisymbrium kind, more pungent, and less suited for beneficial use in health.

LXXXI.

HELIOTROPION (Heliotrope)

Some also call this plant "scorpiouron" (scorpion-tail), others call it "scorpiouros." It grows in marshy places and by lakes, having leaves similar to the one described before, but rounder, and a round fruit hanging down like little warts. The herb, drunk together with its fruit along with soda, hyssop, cress, and water, can expel round worms. Ground fine and applied as a plaster with salt, it also cures warts.

HEPATOREIOS (Eupatorium / Agrimony)

Some call this plant "eupatorion," others call it "hepatitis"; the Romans call it "holosteon," the Egyptians "oxyon." It is a shrubby plant bearing a single slender, woody, upright, dark stem, somewhat hairy — sometimes larger. Its leaves are divided like those of hemp, mostly into five parts or more, resembling those of cinquefoil or hemp; they too are dark and notched like a saw at the tips. A kind of creeping seed grows in the middle of the leaf, somewhat hairy, bending downward, which when dried clings to clothing. The leaves of this plant, ground fine and applied with old lard, heal the most stubborn sores. In addition, the herb itself, drunk with wine along with its seed, helps those suffering from dysentery, liver ailments, and those bitten by venomous creatures. Some call this plant "artemisia."

CULTIVATED CUMIN          WILD CUMIN          ROYAL LILY

The Romans call it cuminum; the Africans "chamact"; it is good for the stomach, and this more so the kind Hippocrates called "barbarikon" — the second kind is the Egyptian. The rest grows in Cilicia and in many other places. Its property is heating and astringent; it is suitable for griping of the bowels and for shortness of breath when given as an enema until evacuation occurs, applied as a poultice together with wine it helps. It is also given for difficulty of breathing mixed with vinegar-water, and for those bitten by venomous creatures together with wine. It is also thought to dry up excessive discharges and swellings of the testicles, mixed with raisins and barley meal boiled and with wax ointment it ripens abscesses. It checks women's flux and nosebleeds when applied with... it changes the complexion to a paler tone when drunk and anointed on.

The Romans call it "cuminum agreste"; others call it "cuminum silvaticum." It grows abundantly, and more vigorously in Carthage of Spain, where it is sold in bundles a span long, having four or five thin leaves, as if sawn along their length, with small round heads at the tip, containing a chaff-like seed, sharper in taste than the cultivated kind. It grows on hillsides. The seed is drunk for... and for shortness of breath with water, and with vinegar for hiccups; it is also good against bruises and stomach queasiness when taken with wine. It relieves bruised eyes when weak, and with raisins it treats inflammations of the testicles particularly, applied as a poultice together with them.

Also called "krinanthemis," also "kallireion," also "lirion," also "sousinon." The prophets [call it] through Ares "sthenis"; the Egyptians [call it] "dyrakrokodilou"; the Egyptians [also call it] "soimpho"; others "damazesin"; also "tiasio"; also "adron." The Romans [call it, text illegible]... also "roza"; also "oinon." The Syrians [call it] "sasa"; [others] "bchadi"; ... "stephano"; "komation"; "lastikon"; the Romans [further names, illegible]...

It has the property, when applied as a poultice, of being an excellent remedy, and it should help against burns that have been scraped; and when made into a juice it is also good for wounds. The juice, mixed with eggs, has a smell, and up to the point of healing... it becomes a remedy that is applied to old sores and wounds to heal them.

CORONOPUS (CROW'S-FOOT)                      CULTIVATED CABBAGE

Some call it ammonios, others astrion;         Some call it "garden cabbage," the Romans
the Africans call it atireitte, the Romans      call it brassica. It is good for the stomach
call it cacciatricem; others call it            when drunk boiled, but bad for the stomach
stillago, others sangynaria. It is a long,      when eaten raw, being sharper than the
low-growing plant lying along the ground,       summer variety. The Egyptian kind is
with deeply divided leaves and a thin,          inedible because of its bitterness. Eaten,
astringent root. It is also eaten as a          it helps those with dim sight and those
vegetable when cooked. The root, ground         with trembling, and taken beforehand it
fine, is good for those with intestinal         quenches the effects of drunkenness and
troubles when eaten.                            wine-fumes. Its broth is better for the
                                                 stomach, though the vegetable itself is
                                                 sharper and more diuretic; when pickled
                                                 it is bad for the stomach and disturbs
                                                 the bowels. The juice of the raw plant,
                                                 taken with iris root and soda, softens
                                                 the bowels when swallowed. Drunk with
                                                 wine it helps against the bites of vipers.
                                                 Mixed with linseed meal and vinegar it
                                                 is good for gout and arthritic joints, and
                                                 applied as a plaster it is good for dirty,
                                                 long-standing sores when anointed on.

It also clears the head when applied with these; mixed with bean meal it brings on
the menses. The leaves, plastered on by themselves or with barley meal, are good
against inflammations and swellings, erysipelas, nocturnal eruptions, and leprous
conditions; combined with other things they also disperse carbuncles. It also checks
the falling out of hair on the head. Eaten together with ash wood it strengthens a
weak voice. Chewed, it restores a lost voice. Taken together with its broth it also
[benefits] the bowels and relieves [various pains]. Taken again, the flower given
after use brings down the afterbirth. The seed, especially that grown in Egypt,
when drunk, shakes out intestinal worms. It is also mixed into medicines for stomach
ailments and cleanses the face; it also helps the ears. The green stalks, boiled
together with the roots and anointed with this and with pig fat, relieve pains of
the side and long-standing aches when applied.

WILD CABBAGE · · SEA CABBAGE · ONION

The Romans call it "brassica rustica." It grows for the most part near the sea and in cliff-like, rocky places. It is wilder than the cultivated kind, and is whiter, hairier, and more bitter; its stalk twists like ivy, which is why it is not eaten. Its leaves, applied as a plaster, have the power to close up wounds and to disperse swellings and inflammations.

Others call it sea-cabbage; the Romans call it "coliculus marinus." The plant called sea-cabbage is a kind of cabbage having long, thin, numerous leaves; each of them grows on small branchlets, like those of the rock-rose. It bears a small white fruit; it has a somewhat salty taste and similarly in its general character. The whole plant, when eaten, is most effective at loosening the bowels; the Italians also preserve it in meat [brine/sauce].

As for the many kinds of onion, the ancients and the Romans call it "cepa." The small kind is sharper than the round, the yellow sharper than the white, the dry sharper than the fresh, and the whole one sharper than the peeled and preserved kind. All kinds are irritant and provoke a windy appetite, are expectorant, diuretic, purgative, good for the bowels, able to open obstructions, promote excretions of various kinds including the menses, and act counter to [snake] venom.

It is applied peeled and dipped in vinegar. Its juice, smeared on with honey, is useful for dimness of sight, for white specks and growths on the eyelids, for ulcerations, and for sore throats; mixed with Christ's-thorn it provokes and brings on the menstrual flow when poured in. It is also good against alopecia, and as a poultice for the head and for dog-bites when mixed with salt and rue and honey — which is why it can heal vitiligo when smeared on with an equal amount of ash... It is also used, mixed with bird's... for repairing the soles/glue of shoes.

At the top it produces umbels resembling those of dill,

like that of cumin and deep-set. It is among the destructive (poisonous) plants,
causing death by chilling (cooling the body). It is counteracted by undiluted wine.
Its juice is pressed out from the topmost shoots before the seed dries; it is then
crushed by pounding and worked together in the sun, and
it is very useful medicinally when dried, mixed with wine
and applied; it is used in pain-relieving remedies and eye-salves. It rolls back
creeping sores (herpes) and erysipelas when applied as a poultice, and it
also stops them. The leaves, applied as a poultice, relieve the pains
of dislocations and similar afflictions. Applied as a poultice it also
suppresses the flow of milk and prevents the breasts
of virgins from becoming inflamed/aching, and makes them remain undeveloped;
it is given to children for the same purpose. The most potent kind is the Cretan
and that grown in Asia.

KENCHROS (Common Millet)

The Romans call it "milium." It is less nourishing than the other cereal grains when made into bread. When prepared as porridge, it binds the bowels and also promotes urination. When cleaned, made into meal, and placed into small sacks and warmed, it is a remedy for griping pains and aches.

KYAMOS (Bean)

The Romans call it "faba." The green (unripe) bean is harder on the stomach and more flatulent. A poultice of beans soothes inflammations resulting from blows, and likewise mixed with barley meal it eases swollen and inflamed breasts, being beneficial, and it dries up milk. Mixed with honey it [relieves] tendinous swellings; with meal it disperses parotid swellings. Mixed with rose oil and [applied], it cures prolapses of the white of the eye and checks watery discharges. When kneaded with wine it sets dislocations and fractures, and serves to bind wounds without the discharge flowing out, applied, having been peeled, to the forehead; and it soothes inflamed testicles when softened in wine. It is also sprinkled, well pounded with dill, upon [the skin] to prevent excessive hair growth when applied repeatedly; and the shelled, powdered husks, sprinkled on, make plucked hairs grow weak and sparse, and also form scabs. Mixed with barley meal and the oil of privet, applied as a poultice, it disperses scrofulous swellings, and the pod (husk) itself, when split, is applied to these. It is also applied to wounds that bleed much. The peeled, split bean, used as it naturally is, also serves cut in half.

CARDAMON (Garden Cress)
It is also called Kynokardamon, Iberis, and Kardamine.
The Egyptians call it Semeth, the Romans Nasturcium.
The best is thought to be that grown in Babylon.
The seed of both kinds is purgative, heating,
pungent, and bad for the stomach; it disturbs the belly, and
drives out worms; it is rare and corrupts embryos;
it stimulates sexual desire. It resembles mustard and rocket
in its effects. When cleansing leprous spots and lichen with honey,
it also melts the spleen when applied as a plaster, and
cleans out abscesses, and clears phlegmy matter settled
from the chest when taken as a drink. It is also an antidote
against the bites of reptiles when pounded and burned as incense,
for it drives reptiles away. It stops falling hair,
and causes carbuncles to come to a head and suppurate when
applied as a plaster with vinegar; it is good
for sciatica, and disperses swellings and inflammations;
it dissolves boils when applied as a plaster with brine,
and mixed with oil it achieves the same effects.
However, it is only moderately effective... [illegible]

COLOCYNTHIS (Bitter Cucumber / Colocynth)
It is also called the bitter cucumber,
also wild colocynth,
also Alexandrian colocynth,
"Zoiroastis,"
the Thracians call it "Talygeneс,"
the Romans "Cucurbita silvatica,"
("Dakoi," "Troutrastra")
It has tendrils and leaves spread
upon the ground, resembling
those of the cultivated cucumber,
but more deeply cut.
It bears fruit like a ball,
bitter in the middle,
very strong; when
it begins to ripen it changes
to a more yellowish color.
The inner pulp of the fruit
is purgative at a dose of four
oboli, taken with honey-water.

When combined with soda, myrrh, and honey it is boiled; when dissolved
dry balls are usefully mixed into enemas for sciatica
and for bowel troubles [illegible] to purge phlegm and bile, and matter...
they also destroy sluggish embryos when applied; for the teeth, it is used
through an enema, similarly also when plastered on externally... boiled
and then rinsed with vinegar; and if one boils it in honey-water...

CRATAEOGONON, OR KRATAIGONON                           CROCUS

It has leaves similar to those of melampyron; several shoots grow from one root, jointed, with a seed resembling millet. It grows in shady and brushwood places, mostly in rocky terrain, and is strongly pungent. It is reported by some that drinking the seed causes a woman to bear male children, if, after her purification, before having intercourse with anyone, she drinks it fasting, in a dose of three obols with two cups of water, for forty days; and likewise the husband should drink for the same number of days.

CROCUS

Castor knows it, as does Cynomorphus; the prophets of the harbor of Heracles also know it. The best is the Corycian, from Cilicia; second is the Lycian, from the Corycus near it, on Olympus in that region; third is that from Aegae in Aeolis. The Cyrenaic and Sicilian varieties are weaker in potency, but juicier and more vigorous in growth, which is why they mislead many people. For medical use, the best is the fresh one, well-colored, not many years old, white, somewhat elongated, whole, full, not having a hollow, airy texture.

When pressed, it stains the hands without being greasy and has a slightly pungent quality — for one that lacks this is either unripe, old, or has been stripped of its essence. This is revealed when crocus paste is mixed in: the genuine kind, when weighed out, balances against a measure of litharge or lead oxide, while the adulterated kind is shown to be dusty by its texture... it should emit fragrance when bent and not crumble when pressed. Thessalus, however, says that it is merely fragrant, and knows it to be dangerous, saying that giving three drachms of it with water is, in truth, diuretic and mildly astringent; therefore it is also used for erysipelas, applied around the area with water, and for rheum of the eyes and similar conditions, it is combined with milk as eye-salves or ear-drops. As for mouth preparations, there is also an unmixed form, the root of this plant, which when drunk with sweet wine promotes urination.

LXXXIX

Clematitis — Another Clematitis — Kestron (Betony)

Some call it "epigetes," the Egyptians "philakouon," the Romans "anbouzou," others "olokroum," or "laktoulaktouke." The clematis sends up a reddish shoot, pliant, with a very sharp-tasting leaf, and is somewhat harmful. It twines around trees like smilax (bindweed). Its fruit, drunk with water or honey-water, purges phlegm and bile downward. The leaves, when made into a plaster, remove leprosy-like skin conditions. It is also preserved with fine oil for eating.

...it is drunk with branches while fresh; it grows in dry places.

The other kind is called by some "philetairion," by others "daphnoides," or "polygonon" by others. It grows along the ground; its shoots are small, about the thickness of a rush, and its leaf resembles that of the bay tree in shape and color, but much smaller. Its leaves and stems, drunk with wine, stop diarrhea and dysentery. Taken with milk and rose oil or henna oil, applied as a suppository, it relieves pains of the womb; chewed, it helps toothache. It also helps when applied to the bites of venomous creatures. It is also said to help those...

Kestron (betony) is found in the coldest places. The Romans call this plant "outeponike." It has a thin stalk, somewhat square and rather larger, with long leaves similar to those of rue, having jagged edges, fragrant; it leans upon a long support. Along the long stalk is where the seed grows in a spike, like that of millet. One should gather the leaves of this plant and dry them; their use is for treatment. The root is thin, like that of hellebore, and these cause phlegmatic purging.

It is drunk with honey-water for ruptures, and for conditions of the womb, for suffocation of the womb, in the weight of a drachm, with honey-water or water; and for those bitten by venomous creatures, even three times with wine.

On Kotyledon (Navelwort), again:

The herb, when applied as a plaster, heals those bitten by venomous creatures. For the same purpose, a dose about the weight of these [seeds/parts] taken with wine is suitable. If someone drinks it beforehand, he will suffer no harm, even if he has taken a deadly poison. It is diuretic and assists the passage [of urine or stone]. It also cures those subject to seizures and the mad, when drunk with water. Taken with oximel (vinegar and honey) to the weight of one drachma, it helps those with liver and spleen ailments. It also aids digestion. If someone takes a piece the size of a reed after dinner, boiled with honey, it likewise relieves acid reflux. It is given to those with stomach troubles — it should be chewed and swallowed, or sipped mixed with wine. For those spitting blood, half an obol's weight is given with a cup of milk; for those with sciatica, with water; and for kidney sufferers and those suffering various pains, as well as for the dropsical, it is drunk at four drachmas' weight with hydromel (honey-water) during fevers, and with honeyed wine when fever-free... it also helps women's monthly courses when prepared with wine, taken in the weight of one scruple. And when four portions are added with hydromel... it helps with consumption as well; for those spitting blood it is combined with honey... The leaves should be kept fresh in an earthenware vessel.

translation: ...they rave, and in whatever quantity, it is softened; the root is similar to the larger one, and the bark is leafless, and it too yields juice when cut. The bark of the root is scraped and preserved in an earthenware vessel, and when pressed... it is written and stored in a clay vessel. The apples likewise yield juice when released; the juice from them is produced when sprouting, and the bark of the root, when stripped off and strung with a thread, is hung up for storage. Some boil the roots in wine and, after straining, store it away, using it for sleeplessness and for severe pains, in whatever way they wish to induce sleep. The juice (opos), mixed with honey-water, purges phlegm and bile; it is like hellebore and from the same source drives out life. It is also mixed into eye-medicines and pain-relieving preparations, and into softening pessaries. By itself, about half an obol's worth applied brings on menstruation and expels the fetus. A piece the size of a finger or an acorn, applied, induces sleep... it is called "elephant-root" when the root, held together, is applied three times at intervals, and it is easily shaped into whatever form one wishes. Fresh leaves are also stored for the same uses; they are useful against inflammations of the eyes and against ulcers; applied as a poultice with... they disperse it, and cure all hardness, abscesses, and scrofulous swellings; applied and rubbed in for six days, they make the ulcer disappear. The crushed leaves are stored for the same uses. The root, mixed with vinegar, heals erysipelas. For bites of venomous creatures, it is applied with honey; with water it disperses scrofula and tumors, and relieves joint pains when combined with barley groats. A kind of wine is also prepared from the bark of the root: one must throw in three... measures of sweet wine, and from it give two cups... for which reason they are accustomed to cut it as has been said before, for they do not perceive the bite because of the resulting drowsiness. The apples, when eaten, and even when merely smelled, cause a kind of stupor, and the juice from them, when taken in excess, also makes one speechless. The seeds of the apples, drunk, purge the womb from wherever it is affected; applied with the fine flour of wheat, they stop discharge. The juice is obtained by cutting around the root in a circle and collecting what drains out — it is thicker than the exuded juice, and more effective, strong in action. Not all roots everywhere yield this juice; practical experience shows the nature of each.

LAMPSANE (Charlock / Wild Mustard)
The Romans call it "napicium," the Egyptians "euthmoi." It is a well-known wild vegetable, more nourishing and more pleasant to eat than dock (lapathon), whose leaves and stem are eaten cooked.

LYKOPSIS (Bugloss / Oxtongue)
Some have also called this plant "aichousa." Its leaves resemble lettuce, but are longer, thicker, and rough, lying flat around the head of the root. It sends up a long, upright, thick stem bearing many rough side-leaves about a cubit long, and upon these small purplish flowers. The root is red and astringent. It grows in plains. When applied as a poultice together with barley meal, the root heals [certain conditions]; and mixed with barley meal it also cures erysipelas.

LAGOPYON (Hare's-foot / similar plant)
Some call it "lagokyminon." It is well known. It has a binding (astringent) power, inducing sleep when drunk with wine. For those suffering from fevers, a small pouch [of it] is hung around the neck; it is also applied against inflammation of the groin (buboes). It grows among rocky places.

WILD / UNCULTIVATED MALLOW

MOLY

The Romans call it "mala ortense" (hortensis)
Pythagoras calls it "anthema"
Zoroaster calls it "diadesma"
The Egyptians call it "chokortin"
The prophets call it "ligospan"
Others call it "ouramyos"
The cultivated kind is more edible than the wild, dry-ground variety; however it is somewhat harsh on the stomach and loosens the bowels, and its stalks even more so; it is beneficial for the intestines and bladder.
Its leaves, when raw and applied as a poultice with a little salt, are said to remove warts (aigilops); mixed with honey they should be used alone, without other ingredients, for suppurations. It also helps when applied as a poultice to bee and wasp stings; and if one anoints oneself thoroughly with it in oil, it protects the whole body. Applied with urine it helps dandruff and scurf. The boiled leaves, applied with oil, help burns and erysipelas.
Its decoction is softening and used as a sitz-bath for the womb, and sometimes for wounds; it is suitable for dysentery of the bowels, for the womb, and for the rectum. The broth made with its roots, drunk, helps against all deadly poisons when one is thirsty; it should be given to those constantly thirsty. It also helps those bitten by spiders and draws out milk (increases lactation). Its seed, mixed with the seed of wild lotus and drunk with wine, relieves pains around the bladder.

Others call it "cherseia" (of dry ground)
Others call it "heliostrophon" (sun-turning)
Others call it "stremphyllion"
The Romans call it "malva rustica"
The Africans call it "boibba"

Others call it "wild gillyflower" (leukoion agrion)
It has leaves like grass (agrostis), similar but broader
Its flowers are like those of the gillyflower
Milky in color... it has pain-relieving properties
It has a slender stalk of about four cubits
At the top it is like garlic-flower clusters
Its root is small, bulb-like, and very white;

Melilot (Μελίλωτον)

Some call it zoodotion, others orthanon, others melilotos; the priests of Egypt call it thermoutis, the Egyptians call it lotos, the Romans call it sertula campana [or similar], others call it tripatium. The best known kind is the Attic, and that growing at Cyzicus, and the one produced at Carthage, saffron-colored and fragrant. It also grows in Campania, near Rome, by the Via [...], though there it lacks fragrance and is without the characteristic scent. It has an astringent power, most of all against every kind of inflammation, especially that affecting the eyes, when boiled with sweet wine and applied as a poultice. Sometimes it is mixed, ground fine, with linseed or with pear or quince [seeds], and used to treat the womb, applied with sweet wine; and fresh honeycomb mixed equally with water is used as a liniment for bruises; with boiled or raw wine it is combined with the aforesaid remedies. It also helps earache when applied with sweet wine as an unguent, and is used as a stuffing for pillows; applied as embrocations with roses and the like.

Melissophyllon (Μελισσόφυλλον, "Bee-leaf"/Balm)

Some call it melitteon, others melittaina, others meliphyllon, others erythromelli; the Romans call it apiastrum, the Gauls call it citrago — "melissophyllon." It is so named because bees delight in it and gather around it; its leaves and stalks are mixed with the hive and are not chewed in the ordinary way but applied like citron-apple. Its leaves, taken in wine, and applied as poultices, are good against the stings of scorpions, bites of spiders, and bites of dogs; and its decoction, used as a gargle, is good for the ears/teeth, and it encourages menstruation. It is good for toothache, and for burns and scalds, and for dysentery. It also helps those suffering from fungal infections and those with stomach cramps; the leaves applied with soda/nitre are good as an expectorant poultice for those with difficulty breathing; applied with salt it disperses scrofulous swellings, and is useful for the pains of nursing [mothers] — such are its applications.

CORN POPPY, APHRODITE'S POPPY, HORNED POPPY

Some call it "oxytonon," the Romans call it "papaver album," the Egyptians call it "panti," because it drops its calyx quickly. It grows among barley in spring, which is when it is gathered. Its leaves resemble chicory, but more deeply cut, smaller and rougher. Its stem is reed-like, upright, and rough, about a cubit tall. Its flower is reddish, sometimes white, resembling the wild anemone's, though its head is more elongated, though less so than the anemone's. The fruit is reddish; the root is long, whitish, bitter, and about a finger thick. Five heads of this, boiled down from three cups of wine to two and given to drink, induce sleep. Taken with honeyed water, as much of the seed as will cover a coin gently loosens the bowels; it is also mixed into honey preparations. The same leaves, applied as a poultice along with the poppy-head, heal inflammations, and a decoction made from them induces sleep.

Some call this one "heraklia." It has a stem about a span tall and very small leaves resembling those of the sparrow-plant. Its fruit is white and foamy. The root is thin, and from it more fruit is gathered once it is fully ripened in summer; if it dries without falling off, it purges by vomiting. A small cup's worth taken with honeyed water is suitable, and is especially useful for such purging in cases of suffocation (choking fits).

Some call this one "paralion," others "wild poppy," others "thalassion"; the Romans call it "fabiolum marinum," the Africans "cissimacesa." It has white leaves, rounded at the edges like those of the wild poppy, with fruit and stem similar to it. Its flower is pale yellow and curved like a horn, resembling that of fenugreek, from which it takes its name. Its seed is small and black, like that of the poppy. The root grows near the surface, black and thick, and it grows in places near the sea and in rough terrain. Its property: the root, when dried and taken with wine up to half a measure, and drunk, treats sciatic and liver ailments, as well as affections of the sides and chest.

translation:
On the garden poppy, also called chamaesyke, also called "mekon ryas," also called "oxytonon" -- the Romans call it papaver, the Egyptians call it nanti.

There is one kind that is cultivated, grown in gardens, whose seed is made into bread for ordinary use, and mixed with honey is used in cakes. It is called "thylax" because of the length of its [pod], which has a head and a white seed. There is another kind, wild, which grows low, bearing its head close to the ground.

Common to both is a cooling property; for this reason the leaves and the poppy-head, boiled in water and drunk, induce sleep. They are also useful, boiled down, against insomnia, and as a poultice. Three poppy-heads mixed with [something] are suitable against inflammations and erysipelas when applied as a plaster. It is also good to pound them while green and shape them into lozenges, drying and storing them for later use.

The heads themselves, boiled until the liquid thickens, make a painkilling remedy effective against sciatica and rheumatic conditions of the joints, as well as disorders of the bowel. Taken in water together with the juice of the black poppy's capsule and seed, and given to drink with wine, they calm the body; in women they check excessive flux. It is also applied as a poultice with water for those who cannot sleep, upon the forehead and temples, and so brings on sleep.

Taken in excess, it thickens and dries [the humors], acting against runny catarrh. It is a remedy that aids digestion and helps coughing and [other ailments], soothing the body when drunk. But it can also harm, causing lethargy, heaviness, headache, and in cases of over-indulgence, disturbed sleep and difficulty waking, and even to miserable [stupor/death].

translation:
...and when mixed with saffron and myrrh and soaked, it is applied to inflammation of the eyes
with yolk of roasted egg and saffron for erysipelas, and also for wounds
with vinegar for gout; and mixed with woman's milk and applied
with a ring, like frankincense, it induces sleep. The best kind is that which
is dense and heavy. And it is somewhat narcotic in smell, bitter, and tending toward green,
easily diluted with water, and of a divine white color, not quickly turning
when it is dissolved, like wax. When placed on a hot stone and smeared,
and lit near a lamp, it keeps a dark flame until the smell's
power is extinguished. They adulterate it by mixing in glaukion
or gum of wild lettuce (oridax). That from glaukion
is somewhat saffron-colored and earthy in taste. That from
wild lettuce is rather reddish...(in) smell and rougher, and that from
gum is without the proper effect and transparent in appearance, having nothing
of the substance, like fat mixed in with it. It is used
for eye medicines on a shell, newly made, until it appears soft and tawny. Erasistratus
however says one must test its use by purchase, for ear pains
and eye ailments, because of the dimming of sight it causes, and as a purgative.
Andreas says that if it were not adulterated, it would blind those anointed
with it, saying that its use is fitting for sleep, but otherwise it happens
to be harmful—what is in fact a lie, for experience disproves those who say
it is beneficial, when, upon testing, the effect of its juice is examined.
It is not out of place to describe the manner in which they collect the poppy juice (opos).
Some, pounding the poppy heads together with the leaves,
press them out with a pestle, rubbing them in the sun, and they form
them into lozenges; such is called "mekonion," weaker than
the (pure) juice. Those who collect the juice must do so after the dew
has dried, and mark around with a small knife an asterisk shape,
so as not to pierce through to the interior;
and cutting the poppy heads obliquely at once, only on the surface,
and when what comes forth dries, the process is repeated again. This too
is found to be of use. One must also store it after shaping it into lozenges. Whenever
one cuts for the juice, one must take care not to let it dry out
too much before storing it as a garment(?) of the labor.

translation:
XCVIII.

[Marginal: onopos]
ONOGYROS (Anagyris)

Some call it "anagyris," others "akope." It is a shrub-like plant with leaves and branches resembling the chaste tree (agnus castus), tree-like, with a strong heavy odor. Its flower is like that of the cabbage. Its fruit grows in long, somewhat rounded pods, variegated, and hardens around what forms at the top [of the pod]. The leaves of this plant, applied as a poultice, disperse swellings. A drachma's weight of it is given to drink with sweet wine for nausea, and to bring down the afterbirth and menstrual flow. For headache it is applied with wine, and it is also used as an amulet for women having difficulty in childbirth. Its fruit, when eaten, induces vomiting.

[Marginal: onopych-]
ONOBRYCHIS

Some call it "onobrycheilos," others "eschasmene," others "hyperikon," others "korin," others "chamaipitys." The Romans call it "oggata," others "brichzalata," others "nopiga," others "iounkinalem." It is sharp and pungent in taste. Its leaves resemble those of the lentil but are somewhat longer. It has a stem about a span high, with a small flower, and it grows in watery places. It has a property that is somewhat astringent; it disperses tumors, and when drunk with wine it treats strangury, and when mixed with oil it induces sweating.

OROBOS
[Marginal: orobos]
The Romans call it "ervum." It is a well-known small shrub with narrow leaves, having seed contained in pods, growing wild, called the kind from which "orobinon" flour is made, which is also suited for medicinal use. It is heavy on the head and astringent; if eaten it causes hunger [craving?], and is diuretic in effect; it stimulates — [and] harms cattle when mixed with their fodder. A kind of coarse bread ("orobinos") is also prepared from it. Such is its nature.

It whitens and nourishes the skin when sprinkled with water, cleansing it of impurities. It is ground together with roasted barley, the shell removed, then crushed and strained through a fine sieve and stored. It induces good sleep, is diuretic, aids digestion, strengthens the weak, and is eaten as food in a drink after meals.

"Jminon ymeron" (Latin gloss of plant name)

CULTIVATED ORMINON (Clary/Sage):
The Romans call it "geminalis," the Dacians "ormea." The cultivated kind, orminon, is in many respects similar to the leaves [of a related plant]; its stem is four-angled, about a half-cubit tall, around which grow projections resembling pods, bending toward the root, in which the seed is of different kinds — for in the wild variety it is found round and grayish-brown, while that of the other (cultivated) kind is elongated and black. It is believed that when drunk with wine it stirs one toward intercourse. Mixed with honey, it clears away white spots (leukomata) on the eyes; applied as a poultice with water, it disperses swellings and inflammations, and the root, likewise applied as a poultice, heals wounds. The wild kind has a stronger potency, for which reason it is mixed into ointments, especially into the glaukion (a preparation).

ORMINON HEMERON (title, in red)                    OINANTHE (title, in red) ✝ [marginal gloss "xanthe"]

DROPWORT (Oinanthe):
Some call it "kerakome" (horn-hair), others call it "leukanthos" (white-flower). Its leaves are like those of the wild carrot (staphylinos); its flowers are white; its stem is thick, about a span long; its fruit is like that of orache (andraphaxys). The root is large, having several round heads. It grows among rocks. Its fruit, stem, and leaves are administered as a drink for difficult childbirth, mixed moderately with wine. The root, taken with wine, is used for strangury (difficulty urinating).

CI.

(Labels: fern [filias/pteris]; scolopendrion; polypodion)

PTERIS            ANOTHER PTERIS            POLYPODION

[Pteris:] Some call it pterion, some pterineon, some dasyklonon, some anasphoron, some blechron, some polyrizon; the prophets call it "Hermes' basin"; the Romans call it filix; also lakoulla; the Egyptians call it philikem, haimaonou. It has no stem, no flowers, and no fruit. Its fronds are about a cubit in size, divided and spread out like a wing, with a somewhat unpleasant smell. Its root is black, elongated, with many branches that are somewhat astringent to the taste. It grows in mountainous and rocky places. Four drachms of this root, taken with honey-water, expel broad tapeworms. It works even better when taken with a little black hellebore — about two doses — and it is said to kill intestinal worms in those who take it.

[Pteris etera / female fern:] Some call it nymphaia pterin, others call it thelypteris (female fern). Its leaves resemble those of the (male) fern, but are more numerous and taller; its roots are long, mossy-looking, blackish with a yellowish tinge, having a reddish color. Taken with honey, they expel broad tapeworms; when drunk in wine in a dose of three drachms, they expel round worms as well. Given to women, they cause barrenness, and if a pregnant woman takes it, it brings about miscarriage. Applied below the knees... as a plaster upon damp or moist areas... it is sprinkled upon beasts of burden... The fresh young leaves, used as a vegetable, and when boiled and eaten, soften the bowels.

[Polypodion:] Some call it skolopendrion, others call it pteris, others polyrizon; the Romans call it filicula or "oak-leaf" (quercifolia). It grows on mossy rocks and on shady cliffs, among the mosses, reaching about a span in height. It resembles the fern, somewhat hairy and divided into segments, though not so finely. Its root is hairy, with tendrils like those of an octopus, about as thick as a small finger; when scraped, it is green within, somewhat astringent, but with a slightly sweet taste as well.

102.

TAMARISK (Myrike)
The Romans [call it] tamariscus. It is well known, growing in watery places. It bears a fruit like a woolly flower, downy in texture. It is similar to the Egyptian kind... Its decoction, when poured on, kills lice and nits. Its wood is useful for those with ailments of the spleen.

MYRRHIS, which some call "marankalysin"
Some call it konile. In stem and leaves it resembles hemlock. It has a somewhat long, tender, rounded root, fragrant when eaten. When drunk with wine it helps those bitten by venomous spiders. It also purges the menses and the lochia. Drunk down in a gruel, it is beneficially given to those suffering from consumption. Some report that certain people drink it daily, twice or three times, with wine, and that it helps during outbreaks of plague and is good against bad odor [or disease].

MYRTLE-LIKE PLANT (Myrta), also called Kameos
Some call it wild myrtle, some call it old-myrtle, some sharp-myrtle, some mouse-thorn, some "barren," some skinkos, some... , some katanballos, some anangelos, some akairon, some oknēron, some [illegible], some ground-pine. The Boeotians call it gorynides. The prophets call it "offspring of Heracles." The Romans call it ruscus. Its leaf is like myrtle, resembling that of fir, sharp and spear-shaped at the tip, and its fruit is round and spherical,

red when ripening, having inside a bony/hard part, and [illegible]... many growing from the same root, hard to break... the root tasting somewhat astringent and yellowish. The leaves and the fruit have the property, when drunk in wine, of promoting urination and bringing on the menses, and of dissolving stones in the bladder. It also cures jaundice, strangury, and headache. It grows in rough, cliff-like, and moist places. The fruit of the root [is] ... when drunk in wine it induces sleep and counters insomnia, and the young shoots, when cooked, are eaten as a vegetable; they are bitter and diuretic.

NYMPHAEA (Water Lily)

It grows in marshes and standing waters. It has leaves similar to the colocasia (kibōrion), but longer and more elongated, rising somewhat above the water; but most of the plant, from the root itself, remains in the water. The flower is white, similar to a lily; when it has faded it becomes round like the head of a poppy — black, within which is the fruit, which is black, flat, dense, and sticky to the taste. The stem is smooth, not thick, rather large, similar to that of the colocasia. The root is black, rough, club-shaped, and large; it is cut in autumn, and when dried and drunk it helps those with intestinal complaints, taken with wine, and also helps those with spleen trouble. It is also applied as a plaster for pains of the stomach and bladder. The root cleanses skin blemishes (alphos) when used with water, and cures baldness when applied mixed with pitch. The root is also useful against nocturnal emissions, for it checks those who suffer from this affliction — it works for a few days, unless one drinks it continually. The seed does the same thing. It seems to be named from "nymphs," because it loves watery places. It is found in abundance near [a certain river] and in the river of Boeotia at Orchomenus.

THE OTHER NYMPHAEA

Some call this one "Nymphon." This nymphaea too is similar to the one described above, but its root resembles more that of the colocasia; however, it has a white and rough root. Its flower is yellow and glossy. The root and seed are good for women's flux (excessive menstrual bleeding) when drunk in wine. It grows in places near the sea, in the region of the river Peneios.

NARCISSUS                                          NARTHEX (Ferula)

[marginal gloss: pakyntos]
[Latin gloss: bulbus narcissi]
[Latin gloss: narcissus]                               [marginal mark]   [Latin gloss: ferula]

Some call the narcissus "anygros," others "autogenes" ["self-growing"], others "bulbos emetikos" ["emetic bulb"], and others "lirion." The Romans call it "bulbus morbitarius." Some have also called this flower "lirion," as though it were a kind of crinon-lily. Its leaves resemble those of a leek, but are smaller and narrower; the stem is hollow and leafless, rising more than a span high, bearing at its top a white flower with a saffron-colored center, though in some varieties it is purplish. The root is white inside, round, and bulb-like; the seed, enclosed in a membrane, is black. The finest and most fragrant kind grows in mountainous regions, while the white variety has a leek-like, grassy smell. Its root, eaten after boiling, or drunk, induces vomiting. It is also good for burns when applied with honey, and for cuts near sinews, acting as a plaster that glues wounds together. It relieves sprains of the ankles and joint pains, and when applied as a poultice it soothes long-standing aches; it also removes freckles. Mixed with vinegar, bitter vetch, and honey, it clears impurities from ulcers and hard, undigested swellings; it bursts and cleans out boils and splinters when applied as a plaster made with wheat flour and honey.

The Romans call it "ferula." Green narthex, when eaten, benefits those suffering from stomach ailments and dysentery. It is given with wine to those bitten by vipers. Used as a pessary with wine, it checks excessive menstrual flow. Its seed, taken as nourishment, is beneficial for those who are hungry [weak from fasting], and when applied as an anointment, it checks sweating when mixed with oil. The stalks, when eaten, are good for headaches, and they are also preserved in brine [pickled] for use.

translation:
CVI.

CYTISUS
(Cytisus, larger-leaved)

It is also called inē, also called great lotos,
also called trifyllon; the Romans call it trifolium
maius. It is a shrub, whitish, like a bramble,
sending up branches a cubit long and even
longer, bearing clusters similar to the lotus
trifolium, but smaller, and having a central
rib. When rubbed between the fingers it
smells of broth, and in taste it resembles
green chickpeas.
Its leaves have an astringent and
dispersive power against swellings when
applied as a poultice; they also move
the urine when their decoction is drunk.
Some plant it near beehives, since it
attracts the bees.

KRISION
(ox-tongue weed)

It is also called trigonon, also called
bouglosson (ox-tongue); the Romans call
it stina mollis. Its stem is soft, about
a cubit long, triangular; below it has
small leaves resembling those of the pomegranate,
with thorny edges, and at intervals along them
guard-leaves. The leaves resemble those of
the bouglosson (ox-tongue), of moderate size,
and the smaller ones are whitish, thorny
toward the tips. The uppermost part of
the stem is round and shaggy, and upon it
are heads tipped with purple,
which open out. Andreas records that
the root of this plant, when its juice
is applied moistened, relieves the pains
of those suffering from ivy-induced
afflictions.

translation:
Chapter 107.

Knekos (Safflower) · Kypairos or Kypēron (Galingale)

[Knekos:] It has long, cut-into leaves, rough and thorny, with stems about two cubits long, also thorny, bearing at their tops heads of considerable size with flowers resembling crocus (saffron). The seed is white and reddish, elongated and angular. Some people use this plant in sauces. The seed, when pounded with honey-water or chicken broth, purges the bowels and benefits the stomach; and when pounded, it softens the bowels. Also, when drunk mixed with almond, soda, anise, and honey, one should take it early in the morning before dinner, dividing it into three or four portions each the size of a royal walnut. It should be prepared in this manner: one xestes of white knekos, three cups of roasted anise seeds (?), one litra of anise, one drachma of foam-of-nitre, forty dates in number. It also coagulates milk; the juice of its seed, mixed with wolf's-bane, also has an effect.

[Kypairos/Kyperon:] Some also call this plant "eryosischoinos," as the Romans call it "aspalathus," and others "kiradikem," others "kyoum." It has leaves similar to leek, but longer, thinner, and harder; the stem is about two cubits or even taller, angular, resembling a rush, not with leaves at the top but with small clusters, and the roots form a pair of tufts, whose use is like that of marsh-reed: elongated, joined to one another, black, fragrant, like Kyperos, bitter. It grows in rough and marshy places. The best kind is the heaviest, the most bitter, and the most abundant, rough, hard to break, aromatic, with some pungency. Such is the kind from Cilicia and from the Cycladic islands.

Its property is warming and opening (anastomotic).

[Main text, on the plant Kyperos/Cyperus:]
It is diuretic, and when drunk it helps those with urine retention and dropsy, and those bitten by scorpions, and for chills around the womb; and when used as a fumigation it helps bring on menstruation. It is also effective, applied dry, for spreading ulcers, but it can be mixed into warming poultices and is also suitable for use in perfume compounds. It is further recorded that another kind of cyperus grows in India, resembling ginger; when chewed it is found to be saffron-colored, and if smeared on it immediately removes hair.

translation:
Leukoion (Stock Gilliflower)
The Romans call it "basilion," also "pulla alba," also "viola alba," also "lygustea," also "viola matronale," also "passarina," also "pulli foura."
Its variety is recognizable by its flower, for it is either white, or saffron-yellow, or purple, or blue — all useful for medicinal purposes. Its dried flowers, boiled, are used for sitz-baths for inflammations around the womb and to bring on the menses. When taken up in a wax ointment, they heal cracks on the finger; mixed with honey, they heal mouth sores. Its seed, drunk with wine in a dose of two drachms, when applied with honey also brings on the menses and the afterbirth. Its roots, applied as a poultice with vinegar, reduce the spleen and benefit those suffering from gout.

Sea Leukoion (Sea Stock)
The Romans call it "viola alba marina."
It has the same properties as the previous plant, though it is not as strongly effective.

Ligustikon (Lovage)
The Romans call it "panakes."
It grows mostly in Liguria, from which it also took its name, in the mountain called the Apennine, which borders on the Alps. The local people also call it "panakes," though not correctly, for it resembles the Heraclean panax (opopanax), and its properties are similar in themselves. It grows on the highest, roughest, and most shaded mountains, especially near mountain streams. It has a slender stem resembling dill, and leaves like those of celery, but more tender; they are fragrant and rather slender toward the top of the stem, and more divided; at the top it bears an umbel, and its seed is black, broad, and oblong. The root, when tasted, is pungent and aromatic like that of fennel, and white in color.

translation: The opopanax (sap) of the Heracleotic Panakes is fragrant. The power of its seed and root is warming; when drunk, it is beneficial for complaints of the internal organs and for difficulty in breathing, and especially for pains around the stomach and for bites of venomous creatures. The root, when drunk, also brings on urine and menstruation, and it has the same effect when applied as a pessary. The seed and the root are usefully mixed with sharp (penetrating) and digestive remedies. It is quite pleasant in flavor, which is why the local people use it instead of pepper, as in their seasonings. It is adulterated by mixing in a certain seed that resembles it, which one can distinguish by taste, for it is bitter. Some also adulterate it by mixing in fennel seed with oil.

Plant labels: Lankiola (Gladiolus) — Lonchitis, the rough kind — Lysimachion

Title: Lonchitis, Lonchitis the Rough Kind, Lysimachion

[First plant – Lonchitis / Gladiolus]
Some call it Kestron, [though] not the Romans — [they call it] Venerica; others call it Lankiola. It has leaves like those of the broad-leaved leek, similar to little daggers, gaping open like comic masks' faces; white [flowers], having from the gaping mouth down to the lower lip something like a little tongue, and seed like a spearhead, triangular within the seed-pods — whence also comes its name. The root is similar to that of wild carrot (daukos); it grows in rough and [illegible] places. This root is diuretic when drunk with wine...

[Marginal note, mostly illegible]
...has a strong/healing power... [called] Lydia...

[Second plant – Rough Lonchitis]
Some call it rough Lonchitis; the Romans [call it] Longina; others call it Calabrina. Its leaves are somewhat similar to those of dill/anise, [and] to the hart's-tongue fern (scolopendrium), but rougher, larger, and possessing it [the healing power] to a greater degree. It has a wound-healing power, reducing inflammation. It also heals sprains/strains when drunk with vinegar.

[Third plant – Lysimachion]
Some call it Lytron; others call its stalks ani[se-like]... reaching the size of those from Chios, and even larger — slender, bushy, with close-set joints, and thin leaves growing out all along, entirely like those of the willow, astringent to the taste. Its flower is reddish or golden in color. It grows in marshy places and near water. The astringent application of its leaves is beneficial for spitting up of blood and for dysentery as a drink, and it checks menstrual flow when placed in front [of the body], and also stops nosebleeds when sprinkled on. The plant is good for wounds and for stopping bleeding. When burned as a fumigant, it produces an extremely pungent smoke, so much so that it drives away reptiles and kills flies.

XANTHION · XIPHION · XYRIS
species, little box, fetid

It is also called Phasganon, also Choiradaleoro [burdock-like plant],
and this is also called, when
the Romans call it, "Lappa."
It grows in moist places and marshes,
having a smooth, angular stem,
and alongside it several branch-joints,
with leaves similar to Andrafaxis (orach),
having notches; in smell it is
quite similar to cress; its fruit
is round like a large hellebore,
sharp, like a plane-tree's
ball, which clings to garments
when touched. For the fruit,
when thoroughly dried,
gathered and crushed and placed
in an earthenware vessel,
can make hair golden if one
applies it during use, taking a bowl's-worth
of it dissolved in rainwater
and plastering it on the head after
cleansing with nitre. Some
also pound it with wine, applying it
as a plaster finely; and it is also
suitable as a remedy, the fruit being
useful for this purpose.

It is also called Anaktorion, also Phasganion,
also Machaironion, also
Arion; the Romans call it "Gladiolus."
It is also called Genalem; because of its
leaf's shape it is named Xiphion
(sword-plant). For it resembles iris,
though smaller and narrower, and sharp
like a small sword; it has a fragrant stem
rising about a cubit, with purplish
flowers standing like small shields;
it has a round fruit; it has roots,
one set upon another,
like small bulbs; of these
one is weak, while the other,
above, is sturdier; it grows mostly
in cultivated fields. The upper
root, applied as a plaster
with wine, can draw out splinters
and thorns when mixed with
honey-wine and wine; it differs
in being applied in such plasters;
they say the root, applied,
also promotes menstruation and
aids in sexual matters.

It is also called Kakos,
also Iris Agria;
the Romans call it "Gladiolus."
It is also called Trimation.
It grows in fields,
having leaves
like little hands,
broader
and jagged at the tip;
it has a stem from the
middle of these leaves
about a cubit
or even thicker,
bearing a flower
like a reddish-purple
bloom,
purple
in color,
with small cups;
its root is
three-fold,
fragrant,
long,
pleasant to taste.

Above, the root taken with wine makes
the smaller amount [of something] useless;
it causes the lower part [of the body] to be relieved
and aids those with intestinal troubles when
given to drink mixed with water.

It draws out wounds and fractures of the skull, and also bones and any foreign object lodged within, by force, when mixed with a third part of copper sulfate (chalcanthum) and a fifth part of centaury root, together with honey. CXV.

Great Sharp Dock (Oxylapathon Mega)    Small Sharp Dock (Oxylapathon Mikro)

Some call it symphyton, others phlommos, others toudel, others
satyrion; the Romans call it romicula, others call it roumex
akidous, others call it roumex kantherinous; the Egyptians call it        The Romans call it rumigastrum
semio, the Africans amoutim.        The Africans call it amouzegaraph.

This oxylapathon grows in marshy places, [and there is] a dry kind, sharper; another kind is cultivated,
unlike the first; the third kind is small, resembling
the small arnoglosson [plantain], low-growing; there is also a fourth kind, which some call oxalis
or anaxyris, or which they call wild dock; its leaves are similar to the small
dock, its stalk not large, sharp, its fruit red and pungent. Upon the
stalk, among the side-shoots, there grows a vegetable from them which, when simply cooked, softens
the bowels; but the raw plant, when applied as a plaster, disperses
honeycomb-like abscesses over time. The seed of the wild kind, and of the oxylapathon, and of the oxalis,
when drunk beneficially with water or wine, helps against dysentery and
disorders of the bowels, and against stomach weakness, and against the sting of a scorpion; and
if one drinks it beforehand, he will suffer no harm if stung. The roots of these, boiled
and applied raw with vinegar as a plaster, heal leprosy and lichen
and leprous nails; but one should first rub the area with nitre and vinegar.
It also soothes itching when its decoction is poured over the area.
It also relieves toothache when boiled in wine and used as a mouth rinse
and gargle. It also disperses scrofulous swellings and parotid tumors when boiled with wine
and applied as a plaster; the spleen likewise with vinegar; and some use it bound
as an amulet against scrofula, hanging it round the neck; and
it stops a woman's flow when applied; when boiled in wine and
drunk, it purges those with jaundice, and
breaks up stones in the bladder, brings on menstruation, and helps those stung by scorpions.

translation:
OREOSELINON · ONOMANON (ONONIS) · OPHIOSKORDON

Some call it wild rock-parsley; the Romans call it apium, the Egyptians call it anonim, Ostanes calls it synobela. The stem is about a span high, single, growing from a thin root; around it are small branchlets and heads somewhat resembling poppy, but thinner; the fruit is oblong, thin, pungent and fragrant, somewhat like cumin. It grows among rocks and in mountainous places.

The fruit and the root have a diuretic power when drunk with wine; they also bring on menstruation. The fruit is mixed into diuretic remedies and antidotes. Let no one be mistaken in thinking that the oreoselinon growing among rocks [is the same plant as true parsley].

Some call it philonitis, others call it homonitis. Its leaves are similar to those of the principal plant, oblong and long, about four fingers wide, lying flat upon the ground, most abundant near the main stem; likewise the fruit, the stem, and the flowers come from a weak, thin, reddish root. It grows slowly in rough places.

The leaves of this plant, drunk with wine, are said to expel the fetus; and they say that if a pregnant woman steps over this plant, it causes a miscarriage.

As it is pounded together with wine or applied as a poultice, it is useful for these conditions and also for the bites of mad dogs; when eaten, it is beneficial for dropsy and for those who have drunk poisoned water; it is also suitable for cleansing/soothing foreign matter, and it clears the arteries (windpipe) and helps chronic coughs.

The Romans call it allium colubrinum; others call it allium viperinum; this is what is called ophioskordon (snake-garlic). It has a pungent, warming power, biting and flatulent, disturbing to the bowels, and diuretic — for those with conditions of the bladder and for growths appearing on the surface of the body.

When eaten, however, it is harmful... but it helps those bitten by snakes and vipers, and those suffering from hemorrhages; nothing else is as suitable. It is taken together with wine.

It soothes when eaten raw or cooked, and kills lice and nits
when mixed with the juice of oregano and drunk; and if mixed
with honey, it heals bruises and alopecia when applied topically.
