ointment and with olive oil, it treats skin eruptions.
It also removes freckles, lichen-spots, and the scaly patches of leprosy,
when applied together with myrrh and frankincense, having been warmed.
Held in the mouth, it relieves toothaches.
It lightens [relieves?] [illegible] a poultice made together with fig
leaves and cumin. As for the hair, [illegible passage about restoring/dyeing it],

PERDIKION

It is also known as Lysimachion, also Sidereitis, also
Bazine, also Chalkis, also Parthenion,
also Elabatine, also Ostilios, also
Herakleion, also Sakina, also Istinagria,
also Polyonymon; the Romans [call it] Herba Callicularia,
also Vitraria, also Parietaria; the Africans
[call it] Tierbitrie. It grows along stream banks, with hairy
stems, a span in height, with leaves resembling [flax(?)]
[illegible], surrounded along the stems with something like seed-
pods that are rough, catching on clothing.
It has a cooling property in its leaves,
and for this reason, when made into a poultice, it is good for
erysipelas, warts, burns, and swellings
that are beginning, and for every kind of inflammation and
wounds. Its juice, mixed with honey,
is beneficial for erysipelas and spreading sores when
applied; and for gout mixed with myrtle wax-salve.
Taken as food like a vegetable, it is likewise beneficial for
those with chronic coughs; its juice, when swallowed,
has a similarly beneficial effect on those with
inflammations — used as a gargle, and as an eye-salve,
and for earache, poured in mixed with rose oil.

translation: It is thick and of many uses. A decoction of the root, boiled down to a third of its original volume, has the power to relieve all the old [ailments]... held in the mouth and used as a rinse [or swished about], it is good for roughness of the windpipe when gargled; it helps a disordered belly and dysentery. Drunk, it helps those with arthritis and sciatica, and as a plaster it disperses scrofulous swellings, hard lumps, tumors, nerve-strains, abscesses, and whitlows on the fingers, as well as warts and freckles. The juice of the root, taken beforehand, acts as an antidote against deadly poisons. The leaves, drunk mixed with honey-water or wine, together with pepper, are given according to the periodic cycle of the fever: for a quartan fever, four leaves; for a tertian, two leaves are to be drunk; for a quotidian, one. It is also helpful against lethargy when drunk for thirty days. The juice of the leaves quickly cures jaundice when drunk for several days, in a dose of about three cups. Mixed with salt and honey and applied as a plaster, it heals wounds and fistulas. It also helps those with intestinal hernia, and stops hemorrhage when drunk or applied as a plaster. It is also used for purgations and to check hemorrhages and menstrual flow [illegible].

CXIX.
115

Polyknemon

POLYKNEMON — UPRIGHT VERVAIN (PERISTEREON ORTHOS) — TRAILING VERVAIN (PERISTEREON HYPTIOS)

Some call it Kleinopodion, some
Polygonaton, some Leios
Elakate, some Icheonymon;
the Romans [call it] Putialogonoria.
It is a shrub-like, bushy plant
with leaves like marjoram, bearing
fruit like Polygonaton,
as with pennyroyal — but not
entirely shady; its small
upper clusters are pungent,
giving off a sweet fragrance.
When applied as a poultice, fresh
or dried, mixed with wine,
it heals wounds; it is also
to be given to drink; it helps
against strangury
and ruptures, given with wine.

Its stem, though plentiful, is found growing from a single root. The leaves, it seems, when applied with rose-oil or olive oil, relieve pain and calm the womb. It also checks erysipelas when applied as a poultice with wine, heals festering sores, draws together wounds, and closes up [wounds] with honey.

Some call it Trygonion, some
Bounion, some Hierabotane,
some Philatrodotis; the Egyptians [call it]
Penpsemirte; the prophets [call it]
Heras-dakryon [Tear of Hera]; some [call it] Haimatitis;
some [call it] Haima-Hermou; the Romans [call it]
Krystagallinakia; some [call it] Feria;
some [call it] Herkoulania; some
[call it] Exouperans; some [call it] Trixalis;
some [call it] Erba palumbaris; some
[call it] Erba sanguinalis.
It grows in watery places; the plant
seems to be named from the fact
that doves like to
spend time near it. It stands about
a span in height, sometimes more; the leaves are
deeply cut, somewhat whitish,
growing singly along the stem,
and resembling, in their arrangement, those of oak,
but narrower, and cut like fig leaves;
somewhat pale; the root slender and rather long.

Some call it another kind, some
Herigenion, some
Chamaidrys, some
Sidereitis, some
Koureitis, some
Persephonion;
some [call it] Dios-elakate;
some [call it] Dichromon;
some [call it] Kallistion;
some [call it] Hipparisos;
some [call it] Demetrias;
the Egyptians [call it] Pemphenphthan;
Pythagoras [calls it] Erysiskeptron;
the Romans [call it] Kinkinnalis;
some [call it] Verbenaca;
some [call it] Loustrago;
some [call it] Kolumbina;
some [call it] Overgitidioum.
Its stalks rise
a cubit high, or even more,
square in shape,
surrounded by [leaves] like those of a vine [illegible].

(Marginal notes: Betony [near the middle plant]; Upright vervain; Betony [near the right plant]; Trailing vervain)

translation: ...fine, with thin purple flowers. The leaves and root of this plant, soaked in wine and applied as a poultice, cause [the condition] to spread/creep; one should bind on, besides, the leaves in the amount of one drachm's weight, together with frankincense, mixed with old wine warmed, taken on an empty stomach for four days: this drink helps old swellings and inflammations. The leaves, applied as a poultice, soothe [pain] and cleanse foul ulcers. When boiled down with wine, it checks the eschars (scabs) in the tonsils and the spreading sores in the mouth when used as a gargle. When taken at a drinking party, the discharge from it produces a heavy, more sedated feeling — so it is reported. It is given to those suffering from tertian fever, [the plant taken] at the third node from the ground together with the leaves surrounding it; to those suffering from quartan fever, [it is given] at the fourth [node]. They call it the "sacred plant" because of its usefulness in purification rites, for sprinkling round about.

translation:
MOUNTAIN RUE          GARDEN RUE          WILD RUE

Also called mountain rue;
the Romans call it
"ruta montana."

The mountain kind is more cultivated, and the garden-grown
kind — the mountain variety is sharper and hotter than the
tame, garden-grown one in its effect; the garden kind is more
edible, especially that which grows near fig trees. Both kinds
are warming, caustic, and binding, diuretic, and bring on the
menses. Eaten or drunk they bind the bowels and act as an
antidote against gas-producing drugs; a dose about the size
of an olive-stone of its seed, taken with wine, and chewed
beforehand — and taken with the leaves, it acts as a sedative.
Taken together with walnuts and dried figs it neutralizes
deadly poisons and the bites of venomous creeping things. In
the same way it extinguishes the generative seed when eaten
or drunk. Combined with this, it helps a customary ailment,
relieving colic and gripes; it is good against pain of the sides
and chest, difficulty breathing, coughing, pneumonia, hip and
joint complaints, feverish chills — taken periodically as has
been said, boiled with honey; and cooked, applied from below,
smeared with honey onto the privy parts up to the anus, as an
application.

The Romans call it "ruta hortensis";
the Egyptians call it "epnubu";
the Syrians call it "harmala";
also called "besasa"; the Africans call it "churba";
it is of two kinds.

Also known as hypericum, also called androsaemon, also
"coris," also called "chamaepitys" by the Romans;
"inderalis," also called "centum nervia," also
"arundinale," also called "rutalco";
also called "rutalcovatica," also "misy";
the Africans call it "chumma-semmaked."

Because of the resin-like substance around its seed,
resembling resin, it is called "tuini." It has small
leaves like rue, a shrubby, brushwood-like plant, rising
to about the height of a hand or three fingers. It exudes a
blood-like fluid from which it is also called androsaemon —
they call it so. It has elongated, rounded pods like barley,
in which grows black seed smelling of resin. It grows on
rough and rocky ground.

It has diuretic and emmenagogue properties; applied, it
is also effective for working purposes; taken with wine
it benefits the hips; it also ripens abscesses within a week
when applied. Its leaves, similarly prepared as a plaster,
are good against burns.

translation: Olive oil also expels worms when applied as a poultice; [it treats] swellings when mixed with honey, and with figs it helps against dropsy; combined with a little flesh[y substance] it is helpful. Likewise it is useful for [illegible] some people [illegible], but others, applied raw and salted, and poured into the eyes, soothe the surrounding pain. Applied as a poultice with barley meal it eases pain, and with rose oil it also helps those suffering from headache. It checks hemorrhages when introduced into the nostrils. For inflammations in the testicles, applied as a poultice with bay leaves, it is beneficial. It also helps against skin eruptions when combined with myrtle wax ointment, and with soda it is useful; when applied around it cures white leprosy (vitiligo). Applied as a poultice together with the same ingredients it removes warts and ant-bite-like growths (small tumors). It is helpful also for lichen (skin disease) when applied with honey and alum. The juice itself, when warmed in a pomegranate rind and applied, is good for earache. When smeared on, it cures erysipelas and herpetic sores; mixed with white lead and rose oil and applied, it heals them. It also counters the odors and acridity from garlic and onions if one anoints oneself with it beforehand. The mountain variety, when eaten much by the kite (bird), and when gathered before flowering for salting, turns reddish, and stains the skin, causing itching and severe inflammation...for the inflamed face and nostrils, it soothes them in this way. They say that the greenery, when scattered, keeps birds away from cultivated land. The one growing in Macedonia along the river Annymos, they say, is deadly when eaten; the mountain region where it grows is full of vipers, and its seed, when drunk, acts upon the internal organs. It is also mixed usefully into antidotes.

translation:
[marginal plant labels: "polygonon arren" (male polygonon); "polygonon, a certain kind," marked with the sign "f"; "polygonatos"]

POLYGONON
MALE               FEMALE POLYGONON            POLYGONATON

Some call it polygonaton, some kynochale, some herakleia, some asphaltion, some cheilophyllon, some klema, some polykarpon, some karkinethron, some myrtopetalon, some knopodion, some zarithea, some pedalion. The Egyptians call it thephin, some call it stemphin. The prophets [priestly writers] call it "blood of the hero," some "mouse's claw." The Romans call it seminalis, some stopinaka, some [name for] creeping things. The Africans call it choudoumiola.

It is a plant having slender, tender branches, many, wound about the joints, creeping, spread flat upon the ground. Its leaves are like rue, but more elongated and softer. The flower is white or sometimes purple. It has a cooling and astringent power. Its juice, when drunk, helps those who spit blood and those with strangury; it is diuretic, and taken with wine it helps against the bites of venomous creatures, and helps before the onset of recurring (feverish) periods.

The Romans call [the female kind] seminalis minor. It is a small shrub having a single, tender, reed-like stem, with joints set closely together continuously, like those of a rope-plant (spartion), and around the joints small leaves resembling [those of the male plant]. Its root is useless. It grows near watery places. It has an astringent, cooling power, producing the same effects as the previous plant, except that it is weaker.

It grows in the mountains, a shrub taller than a cubit, having leaves like laurel but broader, and when tasted sweeter — similar to a quince apple, yet somewhat more astringent besides. At each point where the leaves emerge there are white flowers, exceeding in number those growing from the root. The root is white and soft, long — this is called polygonaton — hairy, heavy-smelling, about the thickness of a finger. It is useful applied as a plaster to wounds, and it also removes blemishes from the face.

PEPLION. 122

Some call it peplas, others iachos,
others polygalon, others ferumbr[...],
others wild sea-purslane,
others galumbron, others pepon,
others sykēn, others mēkōnion,
others hērakleion, others mēkōnaphrō-
dēs; the Romans [call it] portulaca minor,
others laktia. It grows especially
in places near the sea,
a spreading bush, full of
a white [sap], having leaves similar to those of
the purslane, round in shape,
reddish underneath,
with a round fruit beneath
the leaves, like that of the peplos,
fiery to the taste; the root is slender,
rather useless. It is gathered in
summer, dried in the shade
and turned frequently.
Its fruit is stored away
after being boiled. The juice draws off phlegm
and bile when drunk,
a cup's worth mixed with honey-water;
and when mixed with food
it disturbs the bowels. It is also
salted and preserved in brine.

PRASION [Horehound]

Some call it eupatorion, others philophares,
others prapedēlon, others kmēlopodion,
others [...], the leaf-bearing [plant of the] Egyptians,
the astrologers [call it ...], the prophets limataur[...],
others [...] aphedros, others gonosor[...];
the Romans [call it] marrubium, others
labeōnia; the Africans atierberzoia.
It is a bush from a single root, many-stemmed,
somewhat hairy, whitish, four-angled
in its stalks, with leaves set opposite,
somewhat round, hairy, wrinkled, bitter
to the taste, growing at intervals
along the stems; the seed and the
flowers form rough whorls, as it were.
It grows around building-sites and waste places.
Its dried leaves, pounded fine and
boiled together with water, or used fresh
and green, mixed with honey, are given to those
suffering chest ailments, to asthmatics, and to those who cough;
it helps, and brings up quickly from the chest
[phlegm]; mixed with dried iris it is given
also to women who are not being purged [i.e., to induce menstruation],
to bring on the afterbirth, and to women in difficult labor,
and to those bitten by venomous creatures, and to those who have
drunk deadly poison. It is also good for the bladder and
kidneys; moreover the leaves applied as a poultice
relieve spreading sores and soothe pain,
being prepared with honey and applied as a plaster.

PETASITES — PYRETHRON — PRASON (HEADED LEEK / ΚΕΦΑΛΩΤΟΝ)

Petasites: It is also called "moschos," larger than a cubit and about the thickness of a finger, upon which grows a large leaf shaped like an umbrella (petasos), resembling a mushroom cap, which is useful against bad sores and gangrenous ulcers; applied as a poultice it [helps the condition] ... [remainder illegible].

Pyrethron: Also called doryknion, also pyrinon, also pyroton, also pyrophoron, also arnossyreptis; the Romans call it "salivaris," others call it "pastinaca agria" (wild parsnip). It sends up many stalks, like wild carrot or fennel; its umbel is like that of dill, with wheel-like clusters. The root is as thick as a large finger, long, and when tasted it is extremely heating to phlegm and very strongly draws it out. For this reason it also helps toothaches, being chewed, and when burned it draws out phlegm... it is good when [chewed] with olive oil for old pains of the body and for numbness of the limbs...

Prason (Headed Leek): The Romans call it "porrulum." It is flatulent and bad [for the stomach], causes disturbing dreams, is diuretic, mildly thinning, brings on menstruation, but is harmful to the bladder when inflamed and to the kidneys. When boiled together with barley gruel (ptisane) and eaten, it relieves coughing from the chest. Its juice, when drunk, [helps with certain ailments], and its smoke, inhaled, benefits... and so on [remainder illegible].

translation:
[The juice is collected] cut from parts where the stalks are sprouting; famine [goes unnoticed(?)]. The juice, when dried on its surface, turns saffron-colored. They catch what flows out by placing leaves beneath it into a hollowed-out trough, and when it has dried they gather it up. They also cut the stalk itself near the base of the stem, likewise collecting what flows out. Among the roots, the better ones are white, dry, slender, shrub-like, and fiery to the taste, and aromatic. The fruit forms in the middle of the stalk; the one that grows from the side-shoots is without ridges (unstriated). As for the juice, the more bitter one in taste is preferable — white inside, saffron-colored outside, smooth, oily, easily crushed, quickly solidifying, with a strong smell. The black kind is inferior and hard. It is adulterated with ammoniacum gum and wax-salve; it is tested by rubbing it between wet fingers, for the adulteration then becomes apparent.

Its property is warming, thinning, and softening. For this reason it is suited against chills and periodic fevers, spasms, ruptures, pain in the side, coughs, colic, strangury, and the itching that occurs during pregnancy, when drunk with honey-water. It also brings on menstruation and destroys the embryo, and when applied as an enema it disperses flatulence and hardness in the womb. Mixed with honey it is suitable for... and with ointments for scabs. It is also mixed into pain-relieving remedies and head remedies; it helps against erysipelas and is good for carbuncles. It is suitable for gout sufferers when mixed with the sap of the wild grape and held under the tongue. It also relieves toothache when placed among the food. For the eyes it serves as a sharpening ointment when mixed with pitch in a plaster; it is excellent for those bitten by a mad dog. The root, when chewed and applied, brings on the embryo, and it heals old sores and fills in bone-deep wounds with flesh when sprinkled on them. Its fruit, when drunk with wine, brings on the menses; with birthwort (aristolochia), its fruit is good against deadly poisons (venomous bites) and against hysterical suffocation when given to drink with wine.

...the sinews and the head; it becomes useless [if dried out] from behind, the root [remains]. Its stalks also give sap and swell up, and the root is like mandrake, [when] fresh. It acts quickly; its juice kills more swiftly. Sometimes a resinous tear-like substance, similar to frankincense, forms on the stalks and roots. That from Sardinia and Samothrace differs from the one grown in Cyrrhus, [which is] warming to the taste.

It is suitable mixed with vinegar and rose oil for those suffering from lethargy, phrenitis, vertigo, and epilepsy; it produces headaches of long duration. It is good for those suffering spasms, sciatica, convulsions, and in general for all afflictions of the sinews, when applied as an ointment with oil. It is also useful against hysterical suffocation and against fainting fits, drawing [the patient] back to consciousness. It is good against scorpion and wild-beast stings when drunk, and against bad breath, sprinkled with rose oil on the head, or put into food.

It also helps against [certain ailments] when taken with honey, against difficulty breathing and against catarrh and attacks of flatulence; it is suitable, and does no harm, for softening hardened swellings, and is especially good for tetanus [muscle spasms] and the same for diseases of the bladder and kidneys, when drunk. One should also use it for [other ailments]... the root, prepared similarly, acting by itself for the same purposes; its decoction is likewise good.

When it flowers, it is gathered impure and fine; its ash is likewise [used] at that time and, when sifted, [applied] as a powder. It is also mixed with plasters and warming poultices made from it. One should choose the fresh, unspoiled kind within [a certain] month. The juice is also mixed into drinks, with almonds or pears, or [taken] warm with bread in the morning.

translation:
126.

Paronychia · Polion, the Mountain kind · Polemonion

[Paronychia] is also known as "akidotos," also as
"neuras," also as "phrynion."
The Romans call it "buginalia."
It grows among rocks,
a small shrub resembling
pepper, but smaller,
and it is used with its larger
leaves. When applied as a
poultice, it heals whitlows
(paronychiae) and hardened sores.

The second kind is not as strong in smell as the first
but is weaker in its properties. Its decoction, when drunk,
can relieve the bites of venomous creatures, and helps
those with dropsy and jaundice. For those lacking appetite
it sharpens it; but it is a cause of headache and upsets
the stomach, disturbs the bowels and the menstrual flow.
When strewn beneath, it drives away wild beasts, and when
applied as a poultice it closes up wounds.

[Polion] is also called "teuvrion," also "pheuxaspidion,"
also "achamenis," also "ebeneitis," also "melosme,"
also "belion," also "leontychion."
There are two kinds: one is the mountain kind,
which is also called "teuvrion," and this is the one
in use.
It is a small, slender, whitish shrub,
about a span high, with leaves... bearing
small fruit-heads clustered atop like corymbs,
somewhat resembling rosemary,
with a heavy but pleasant odor. The other shrub...
[illegible]

[Polemonion] is also called "philetairion."
The Cappadocians call it "cheil-..."
[illegible]
"chrysattalmion"
[illegible]
Its leaves resemble those of rue,
growing upon [illegible]
stalks upright, resembling
knotgrass; it has
a beautiful appearance upon
its clusters, round like corymbs,
with a black root, which some liken
to the sparrow-plant (strouthion).
It grows on rugged mountains
in rocky places.
Its roots are taken
with wine, and are good for dysentery;
they also help with [something]
mixed with water,
and with vinegar
taken to the weight of a drachm.

It is also said to be effective against the sting of a scorpion:
those who carry it are said never to be harmed,
and even if stung, to suffer nothing.
It also relieves toothache when chewed.

RHODODAPHNE (Oleander):
Some call it porgos, some theidaimos, taris,
Some call it nerion, some rhododendron.
The Romans [call it] rodorandrum, others laurorodon;
the [people of] Lycnos [call it] kmani, the Egyptians schinph-
loroi [call it] rhododaphne. It is a shrub re-
sembling the almond tree, but taller and
rougher, having leaves like oleander, and
rose-colored flowers; its fruit is wrapped like a horn,
with a woolly down beneath,
similar to that of thistle-like plants.
The root is slender and long, woody, and when
tasted is bitter. It grows in places
by the sea and along rivers.
The flower and the leaves have the
power to destroy all animals,
but to preserve humans when
taken with wine against the bites
of venomous creatures, especially when rue is
mixed in. But the weakest of animals,
goats and sheep, if they drink water in which
it has been steeped, die...

It is good for weakness of the stomach, for those afflicted with
kidney and liver ailments, for griping pains and
for swelling of the chest and the hypochondrium when
used with safety; it relaxes and helps those who suffer from
asthma and similar troubles.

RODIA RIZA (Rose-root):
Some call it rodia, others call it
by another name. It grows in Mace-
donia, resembling a chestnut,
but lighter and
more porous in structure.
When ground with rose [oil]
it produces a fragrance.
It is useful for those
suffering headaches,
when moistened with water
it is thinning, and when
applied to the forehead
and the temples it brings relief...

In time it produces [an effect];
with a small amount it
is chewed and taken in due season,
used against bone fractures and
such swellings...

RADISH (RAPHANOS)                          WILD RADISH (RAPHANOS AGRIA)

There are many kinds of "eryngion." The Romans call it "radix," the Thracians... the Africans call it "thorphath." It also produces wind, is good for the stomach, yet not very nourishing for it. It is good for belching and for urination, and loosens the bowels. It should be taken especially raw, since cooking makes it float up the food [in digestion]. It is also suitable for those about to vomit, taken well-boiled. Taken precisely in the proper way, it helps those with coughs and those who develop phlegm quickly through the night. Its peel, taken with oxymel (vinegar and honey), is more emetic. It is good for dropsical patients when applied as a plaster, and it is also helpful for those with spleen trouble when mixed with honey. It removes spreading sores and bruises, and helps those bitten by vipers. It also thickens hair in cases of alopecia, and removes freckles when rubbed on with bean meal. It helps those suffocating from fungus poisoning, brings on menstruation, and its seed is emetic, diuretic, and rarely purgative when drunk with vinegar; it vigorously scarifies gangrenous sores and helps those with quinsy (throat inflammation). Boiled with oxymel and warmed, it is good as a gargle, and when drunk with wine, it helps against the bite of a horned viper.

[Continuation at bottom, shared between columns]
...stir together with water, and for one who understands the illness, card finely. Three half-obols of this, taken, purge both upward and downward.

WILD RADISH:
It is also called "mountain radish," also "wild," also "ischas," also "wild earth-acorn," also "linozostis" by some. The Romans call it "radix silvestris." The Africans call it "thorphath," the Carians call it "sadoi," others "klonides." It is said to have branches about three spans long, with small reddish leaves resembling those of wild dill, but these are more elongated and narrower on this plant; the fruit is small, and the root is similar in shape to that of a turnip, somewhat rounder and resembling the shape of a foot, having in places a white bark. 

When the upper part of this root is taken, it induces vomiting of bile and phlegm; but the parts near the root purge downward. When the whole root is taken, it stirs up both kinds of purgation. Some wish to preserve it by cutting up the roots and placing them into a vessel.

[Final lines, shared]
...mix together with water, and for one familiar with the dosage, grind finely. Three half-obols of this, when drunk, purge both upward and downward.

CXXXIII.

Satyrion            Satyrion, another kind          Satyrion, the red

SATYREION·          SATYREION, ANOTHER KIND·        SATYREION, THE RED·

Some call it orchis, some kynosorchis, some call it heteron, some priapeion, or priapiskos, some call it morion; the Romans call it "aerian satyrion." It has leaves spread around the stem on the ground, resembling olive leaves but longer; its stem is about the size of a shrub's branch, and sometimes larger, bearing purple flowers; its root is bulb-like, elongated like an olive altogether, one part above thinner, the other below thicker, one firmer, the other softer and more delicate. When eaten raw it tastes like a bulb. It is said that the larger root, if eaten by men, produces male offspring; the smaller one, if eaten by women, produces female. It is also recorded that if the larger of these roots is given to drink in a little milk, it stirs sexual desire, while the dried one checks and quenches sexual desire, so that one is neutralized by drinking the other. It grows in sandy and marshy places.

Some call it trifyllon ("three-leaved"), because it bears many leaves, three together, close to the ground, broken off, similar to the dock plant; the stem, however, also rises up, small, about a cubit high. Its flower is like a lily, white; the root is bulb-like, like a reddish apple; inside it is white; when tasted it is sweet and good-flavored. This one, taken in dark wine, is astringent and binding; and if you wish to prevent intercourse, they say this plant has the power to stop it.

Some call it satyrion erythraikon (the red Satyrion), others call it melion-in-water, others "tension-giving" (entatikon), others priapiskon, others satyriskos, others "orchis of the satyr"; the Romans call it mollartikon or alumbeneris. It bears seed similar to flax-seed, but larger and glossier, and purplish. This is also said to stimulate sexual intercourse, strongly, like the scincus (skink) does. There is a difference in it: one kind is pale yellow and tender, and reddish; the other is white inside; when tasted it is pleasant and sweet. It grows in sunny and mountainous places. It is recorded that if its root is taken in the hand, it arouses desire for intercourse — much more so if it is drunk mixed with wine.

Scorpiouron. Scorpiouron, another kind. Scorpioeides (scorpion-like plant).

[First column - on Scorpiouron proper]
It is also known as heliotropion, also called heliotropos, also dialion, also heliopoun, also scorpioktonon (scorpion-killer), also wild sesame, also scorpiou-ourani-kalou, from the shape around its flower, and heliotropon from the fact that its leaves turn all around toward the course of the sun, and it moves with it. Its leaves are like those of basil, though narrower, larger, and thicker. Its branches grow from the root to about three or four spans, and from these the branches produce more at the top. The flower is white, somewhat purple, and curved like the tail of a scorpion—hence the name. The root is thin and without much strength. It grows in rough places.

About a drachma's weight of this, boiled and given as a drink, purges phlegm and bile from the bowels. It is also useful for those stung by scorpions when drunk with wine, and applied as a plaster. It is also worn as an amulet to assist in childbirth. They say that four seeds of its fruit, taken with wine before the hour of the illness begins (counting from the fever's onset), stop fourth-day fevers, and three seeds stop third-day fevers. The fruit, when applied as a plaster, dries up ant-bites, warts, boils, and nighttime skin eruptions. Its leaves, applied as a plaster, help with gout, sprains, and the "dog-star" ailment in children. It also stimulates menstruation and expels the embryo when applied.

[Second column - on the "other" Scorpiouron]
It is also called the small heliotropion. It grows in marshy places and by lakes, having leaves entirely like those described above, but rounder, and a round fruit hanging down like little warts. A large quantity of its fruit, taken with nitre and hyssop and cardamom in water, expels both flat and round intestinal worms. Applied as a plaster, it also removes warts together with the skin growths.

[Third column - on Scorpioeides]
This is a small plant having few leaves, and its seeds resemble a scorpion's tail. It helps greatly those who have been stung by scorpions.

136

Sideritis; Struthion; Strychnos, the black garden kind

Some call it Herakleion; the prophets [call it] "offspring of the scorpion"; others "blood of Titan"; others "tail of the scorpion"; Pythagoras [calls it] Panmoron; Andreas, Xanthophanes; Osthanes, Boethelaion; the Egyptians, Senephthiomor; the Romans, Verbenaca; others [call it] Mulgendrum; others, Solastrum; others "ox-giant," Silvaticum; the Africans, Oudonnin. It resembles leek, but is similar in its upper parts to leek; however its force seems to show more clearly in the leaves. The stems are rather thick and rough, four-cornered, a cubit long, somewhat thorny, not pleasant [to handle], astringent; on them, at intervals, are round whorls like those of horehound, and the seed is black. It grows in rocky places. Its power, when the leaves are applied as a poultice, is to be binding on wounds and to check inflammation.

Some call it Kedros; others, Chalbane; others, Strouthokamelos; others, Chamairytron; the prophets, Chalirygon; the Romans, "Radix Sandia"; others, "Erba Lanaria"; the Egyptians, Oino; the Africans, Souri. It is well known that the wool-workers use its sharp root for cleansing wool. It is diuretic, helps liver complaints, coughs, difficulty breathing, and jaundice; one spoonful taken as a drink with a little honey helps, together with asparagus, and relieves pain in the loins; it breaks up stones and promotes urination; applied, it reduces an enlarged spleen; mixed with a softening agent it also serves as a pessary; it destroys the embryo when applied... it dissolves tumors and is used also in enemas.

Some call it Imeron; the Romans, Strumbum; others, Koukrybelon; the Egyptians, Allo; [others], Skoubolou; the Africans, Astromounim. Bydatimos is its [other name], the greater; it has small leaves, similar in shape, with darker stalks; its berries are larger, rounder, green turning dark and yellowish-red when ripe... [several lines of uncertain content follow, including notes in a later hand] ...concerning its taste and properties: it has power to bind and cool; applied as a poultice it cleanses foul sores and promotes healing; mixed with vinegar it purges matter.

translation:
STOEBE
Some call it stoibion,
the Romans call it stippa.
Its fruit, when ripe,
along with its leaves, is burned,
whence it is also useful for those
suffering from dysentery when burned.
It is also burned and applied to ears
that are discharging reddish matter.
The leaves, when applied as a plaster,
help with blurring of vision in the eyes
caused by a blow, and it stops
hemorrhages.

SPHAIREITIS
Some call it Keladeitis, others
Alexikakos, others Moly;
the Romans call it Vernalis, others
Sostralis, others Vapularis;
the Egyptians call it Anouchi.
It has leaves like grass,
with flowers resembling... white,
similar to white violets, milky
in color, somewhat more... than
...stalks that are thin,
white, about a span long,
and others larger, with many
small thin leaflets. At the
tops of the stalks there is
something like a garlic clove, or a small
bulb-like root, very good
for closing the womb when crushed
and applied with iris ointment on top.

SCILLA (Squill)
Well known.
It has a sharp property,
very fiery; it becomes beneficial
when roasted.
It is styptic. It is sometimes
coated with dough and placed
into an oven, or buried in
charcoal embers until
it is thoroughly roasted;
and once the outer covering is removed,
if it has not become soft,
it is roasted again, wrapping it
in more dough, so that
we may fully roast it;
for if not roasted this way,
it is harmful, especially
to the internal organs.
It is also [treated] in a covered pot,
sealed with clay and placed
into an oven. The usable part is taken from its cut,
the outer parts being removed, and it is boiled
after pouring off the first water, then soaked again in fresh water
until it is no longer bitter or sharp; the water is drained off,
and first it is dried in the shade after being cut,
and divided in such a way
that the cut pieces do not touch each other. This then
is used with wine and oil, and the squill-based (preparation)...

translation:
Sikys agrios (Wild Cucumber)

Also called elaterium, also grynos, also balis, also synkrisis, also boubalion,
also skorpion, also perombron, also peukedanon, also notion;
the Romans call it ankentoum or cucumeres agrestikum or agrestem;
the Africans call it koussimezar. It bears fruit not much different from
the cultivated kind, but smaller, having many leaves, and stalks similar
to those of the cultivated plant. Its root is white and large. It grows
in untilled ground and in vineyard areas. The whole shrub is bitter.
The juice of the leaves, dropped in, is good for earaches. The root,
applied as a poultice with barley meal, disperses all old hard swellings;
applied with resin it breaks open boils. Boiled in vinegar and applied
as a plaster it relieves gout and sciatica. It is used also as an enema,
and for toothache when warmed and applied. Dried and powdered,
it cleanses leprosy-like spots and scabs, and removes black scars
and blemishes from the face. Its juice is useful in a dose as small
as half an obol, and the bark too, about a quarter of that amount.
It purges phlegm and bile, and is especially good for those with dropsy,
though it irritates the stomach and causes the purging to be rough.
It should be given, about one dram's worth, mixed with two measures
of sweet wine, especially to the healthy, and given from a cyathus
to those suffering from it... The elaterium prepared from the fruit's
juice is made in the following way: they gather the wild cucumbers
while still green, before they are fully ripe, and leave them overnight;
then they place a fine sieve over a vessel and, cutting them open with
a knife, holding them with both hands over the sieve, they squeeze out
the juice of the cucumbers so that it drips down into the vessel placed
beneath. What is pressed out is left to settle, and the thick part
that gathers from the cucumbers is dried in the sun after being strained
through a sieve, and this, once dried into cakes, is kept for use.

translation: And when the moisture that is drawn off has set, [the physician] gives the order. One strains it off and does this just as those who prepare it carefully [instruct], the settling [of the liquid is collected] with... and they shape it into little round tablets (trochiskoi). Some, in haste, while the moisture is still present, spread out a piece of linen over it when it has dried and press it into the middle, and squeezing it over the cloth, they pour the juice (the elaterium) together with its moisture onto it, and leave it to dry as has been said before. Others, having added a little water, wash it by changing the liquid repeatedly; others, at the last washing, pour on diluted wine instead. The best kind is thought to be that made with the white [variety], which is not too moist, light, smooth, and very bitter to the taste, and is rather dry; but the greenish and rough kind, and that which is heavy and ashy and full of lumps, is useless and inferior. Some mix in the juice of the cucumber as well; others add starch to make it more pleasant, keeping the preparation white and light. For purging purposes it remains usable for two years; the standard dose is one obol, the smallest amount is half an obol — for infants, a mere grain weighing as much as a "lentil copper" (dolichalkon). It is taken to purge both upward and downward, drawing off phlegm and bile; it is best for those with difficulty in breathing, when purged through this means. If one wishes to purge the bowels, mix a double portion, combined with... as much as needed, and make it into pills (orobia) the size of a chickpea and give them to swallow. Give also a cup of lukewarm water to drink afterward. But to induce vomiting, mix it with water and smear it, lukewarm, under the tongue. For those who are over-purged, give continually a little oil mixed with wine, for this will stop the vomiting without the purge itself abating. When vomiting does not subside, give cold water, and barley groats, or vinegar-water, and fruit, and whatever the stomach can bear should be given, but not too frequently. One should also be aware that elaterium provokes menstruation and expels embryos. Applied as a pessary, or poured, mixed with milk, into the nostrils, it cures jaundice and relieves chronic headaches. For those with quinsy (sore throat), a liniment prepared with it and honey or ox-gall is useful as a sternutatory (causing sneezing). A portion the size of a bean of the root of the cucumber, given with water and honey, finely ground, in the weight of a drachm, mixed [with wine,] purges likewise. And if someone wishes to vomit gently after dinner, two obols' worth suffices.

GARDEN MUSTARD · WILD MUSTARD OR SCORDION.

The Romans call it napy; the Greeks, mustard (sinapi). Choose
the kind that is not overly dried out or brittle, but plump, so that
it appears green and juicy inside; for such mustard is fresh
and at its best. It has the power to warm, to thin, to draw out,
and to clear phlegm when chewed. The mustard seed, mixed
with honey, when gargled, is good for inflamed tonsils and
chronic roughness of the windpipe, and for hardened swellings.
When ground fine and applied to the nostrils, it induces
sneezing, and it rouses women suffering from hysterical
suffocation. It is also applied as a plaster for alopecia (hair loss).
It cleanses the face and removes bruises when mixed with
honey; with fat it forms a salve; with vinegar it is used for
leprosy and for stubborn wild lichen-like skin eruptions when
rubbed on — it causes irritation — and it helps with menstrual
periods. Dried and applied as a plaster, it draws things out
powerfully, and without salt it is mixed as a remedy for
deafness and ringing in the ears when applied with fig. Its
juice mixed with honey is good for dimness of vision, and for
wounds; it is also smeared on the eyelids. The juice is
extracted while the seed is still green, and the rest, once
pressed, is dried in the sun.

TRIFOLIUM, OR MINYANTHES, OR ASPHALTION          TRIPOGON          TYPHE

Some call it "oxyphyllon," others "minyanthes,"
others "asphaltion," others call it "cnecion";
the Romans call it "trifolium acutum,"
others "trifolium odoratum."
It is a shrub a little more than a cubit tall, having thin,
solid, black, rush-like branches bearing side-shoots,
on which grow three leaves resembling those of
each sprout; their smell, when freshly sprung,
is like that of rue, while the asphalton type
produces a purple flower
and a broad seed, flat on the one
end like a little horn. The root is thin,
long, strong, and firm. The seed and the
leaves, taken in water, help those
suffering from epilepsy, dropsy, and hysterical complaints — give
one third of the seed and four parts
of the leaves. They also promote menstruation when drunk, and help
those bitten by wild creatures; the leaves, softened
with wine, are said by some to be useful; a decoction of the root and leaves,
poured over snakebite wounds, relieves pain of the spine. If
one has another sore, the same treatment helps when poured
over the affected area. Some give it to drink — on the third day three leaves and three seeds
in wine, on the fourth day four, since it causes the (fever) periods to dry up; its root
is also mixed into antidotes.

TRIPOGON
Also called "tetraporona" or "come" by some; it has a short stem,
leaves like those of crocus, a long, upward root.
On top of the stem is a large calyx, from the top of which
grows a black fruit — hence its name. It grows
in many places.

TYPHE
Some call it "typhe." Its leaf grows up resembling
that of the cypress, with a smooth stem,
entirely surrounded at the top by
a dense flower-head, which some call
"anthele." The flower, mixed
with much fat or oil, cooked together,
heals burns. It grows in marshy
and stagnant-water places.

[Plate heading] 142.
tripolion

TRIPOLION

Some call it Psyche, others call it Myris,
others call it Potamogeiton, others
call it Stachyitis; the Romans
[call it] Trifolium maius.
It grows in places near the sea,
places which the sea washes over
and then recedes from; it has leaves
neither in dry land nor in the sea.
It has leaves like woad [isatis], hard,
rather thick, with a stem about a span high,
split above.
It is recorded that this plant's flower
changes color three times a day:
white in the morning,
purple at midday, and
reddish-purple in the evening. Its root is white,
fragrant, and warming to the taste;
drunk in wine,
in the amount of two drachmas, it moves
the bowels and brings on urine.
It is also cut for use as an antidote
against poisons.

triphólion [marginal gloss, meaning "trefoil"]

PITYMALLOS CHARAKIAS (Tithymalos Characias)
pitymallos characias [marginal gloss]

12                              anabula maior [Latin marginal gloss]

Of Tithymalos there are seven kinds: one
called the male, Characias, and one which some
call Komites, another Amygdaloides, which
is also called Kobios; another is the female kind,
Myrtites, which some also call Karyites;
another is the Paralios, which some have called
Tithymalla; another is the one called Heliokotios;
another is Kyparissias; another Dendroeides;
another Platyphyllos.
The one called Characias has a stem
more than a cubit high, red, sharp,
and quite pungent, full of white [latex].
The leaves around its branches are similar to the olive's,
but longer and narrower. At the
tips it is woody, and at the top of the stems
it bears a tuft like a rush, with thin
hollow parts beneath it, similar to cups,
in which the fruit grows. It grows
in rough and dry places.
It has a purgative power as a latex,
cleansing the lower bowels and
bile, when taken in a dose of two obols,
mixed with a little wine.

translation:
...with honey-water, and it also moves [the bowels]. The sap is gathered after the vintage, once the branches have been collected and cut off; the branches should be left leaning against something. Some mix in bean flour and mold it into shapes the size of beans. Some let it drip onto things being dried, letting it coagulate for three or four [days], and then, once dried, they store it. For it is soft when rubbed [with the hands], which is why it is shaped in a mortar and then stored.

When extracting the sap, one must not stand facing the wind, nor bring the hands to the eyes. Rather, before gathering the sap, the body should be anointed with tallow or oil mixed with wine, especially the face and the genitals, for the sap roughens the skin and also irritates the throat. For this reason, pills [made with it] should be coated with wax or honey before being swallowed in this way. Two or three figs taken are sufficient for purging.

Fresh sap applied with oil in the sunlight is good for the eyelids and for hair: it both affects the fine, blond hairs that grow in, and eventually removes all the hairs. It is also put into decayed teeth to relieve pain. Applied with wax, it is also good for chilblains, carbuncles, spreading sores, gangrenous ulcers, and fistulas.

The fruit [of the fig], gathered in autumn and dried in the sun, is lightly pounded and crushed, then gently boiled, and stored once cleaned. The leaves are dried in the same way. The fruit and the leaves have the same effect as the sap itself when steeped — half an oxybaphon's worth of the blossom [being used]. Some pour this over [preparations], mixing it with thin milk. Also, the root, applied as a plaster, moves the bowels. Boiled with vinegar and used as a mouth rinse, it relieves toothache [tooth pain].

[Marginal plant labels: "Tithymalos of Kyparissias," "Tithymalos Dendritis," with a Latin annotation in a later hand noting "tithymalos with large leaves."]

TITHYMALOS          TITHYMALOS          TITHYMALOS
OF KYPARISSIA          THE TREE-LIKE ONE          BROAD-LEAVED

It sends up a stem a span long, or even longer, somewhat reddish, from which grow leaves like those of the pine tree, though more delicate and finer. On the whole it resembles a young pine shoot, from which it also got its name. It ripens, and it too has a white sap. Its potency is similar to the ones described before it.

The one that grows on rocks, called tree-like, is leafy all over from above and much-branched, full of sap, with reddish branches, around which the leaves grow like fine myrtle leaves. Its fruit resembles that of the "charakios" plant, and it brings about healing in the same way as the others; it works just as effectively as those described above.

It resembles bark; its root, when roasted, and its leaves taste bitter and are harmful to the stomach. It upsets the bowels, and when drunk it works on the stomach, and they make it into tablets [for such purposes].

HYPEREIKON (St. John's Wort)    HYPOKYSTIS    HYPOKYSTIS, the other kind    HYSSOP

Also called askyron, also askyroeides, also androsaimon. This too is a kind of hypericum, differing in its shrub-like stems, and sprinkled with thin leaves and small, dark flowers, and a fruit similar to that of hypereikon. When the seed is rubbed between the fingers it gives off something like wine-colored [dye], which is why it is itself called androsaimon ("man's blood"). This fruit is also good for sciatica, taken in a drink of two kotylai of honeyed water. It also purges much bile and waste if given continually, until the desired effect is known. It is also good for burns when applied as a plaster.

Also called hypokyssis, also throbneron, also thorybneron, also kytameinos, leon, also leontias, also dionysias, also thyrsion.

It grows beside the roots of the cistus (rock-rose), the plant called hypokyssis; one kind is tawny, another white, having many leaves, from which juice is pressed out like that of acacia. Some dry it, then soak it and crush it and boil it, and prepare it in other ways as is done with lycium. It has the same properties as acacia, but is more astringent and more drying, being effective for those with intestinal and dysenteric troubles, and those spitting blood, when drunk. It also checks excessive menstrual flow in women.

Also called diobion, also kytinon, leafless, also thyrsion, also thorybneron, also knorobneron — the people of Africa call it bimesade.

[The people of] Rome call it ysopum; also called later, also kassiada, ligyrio, saem; itol. It is well known in two forms, for one grows in the mountains, while the other is cultivated in gardens; the better one is that which grows in rocky places. It has a warming property. The uncooked kind, taken with water, cleanses and ... ; drunk, it helps those with lung ailments and bodily complaints, chronic coughs, and orthopnea (difficulty breathing); it also kills worms. Taken with honey it clears phlegm; it also thins thick humors generally.

Its preparation is written up together with [that of] oxymel (vinegar-honey mixture).

HYPEKOON
Some call it "hypophēōs."
It grows in sown fields
and in cultivated land,
having leaves like rue,
small shoots.
It has a power
analogous
to that of the poppy's
juice. —

HYACINTH
Some call it "helionēas," others
"porphyranthes"; the Romans
[call it] "vaccinium," others
"hyacinthium."
It has leaves like those of the bulb,
a stem upon a smooth shrub,
thinner than a small
finger, bearing a tuft
lying curved upward,
of more purple-colored [flowers];
its root is also similar
to the bulb, which, plastered
on with wine, is believed
to preserve the modesty (chastity) of children,
and also induces
sleep and brings on urine
when applied, and is useful
against spider[-bites].
Its fruit is more astringent;
it is suitable for antidotes
and cures jaundice
when drunk with wine. —

translation:
With a purple-colored [appearance], the leaves similar to smilax, the seed black, and the capsules hard and thorny. The one from Galinia has white flowers, and the leaves are also whiter overall; the seed grows under the flowers like that of erysimon. Both of these kinds cause madness and are harmful to dropsical patients, but they are useful for the treatment of the liver. The third kind is oily and soft and fibrous, having white flowers and white seed; it grows beside the sea and in straits. If this is not available, one should use the flowering kind; the black-seeded one should be rejected.

The soft fruit yields juice, as do the leaves and stalks when pounded; dried in the sun, its moisture is used for some conditions because it is prone to putrefaction. The seed also yields juice when pounded dry and hot water is poured over it and pressed out; this pressed juice is always better and more effective against pain than the drink. The green part, when pounded and mixed with wheat flour, is formed into pastilles; this is suitable, [as is] the first extract and that made from the dried seed, for eye-salves against pain and inflammation, and for earaches, and for conditions of the womb, mixed with flour or barley meal, against inflammations and swellings of the eyes and other such things.

The seed itself, prepared, is good against cough and catarrh, and discharge of the eyes and painful conditions, and for women's disorders, and against hemorrhage—about one obol's weight taken with poppy seed, or with honeyed water. The seed is suitable for gout, swollen testicles, and breasts swollen after childbirth, applied as a smooth poultice; it is also usefully mixed into other pain-relieving poultices, and the pounded leaves are usefully mixed into all pain-relieving poultices along with barley meal, and also by themselves. Fresh leaves applied as a poultice relieve pain in all cases; taken three or four times in wine, they cure persistent fevers. Eaten cooked as a vegetable, a bowlful produces a moderate laxative effect on the bowels. Anyone who has a sore or burn on the chest is helped by the same remedy at once. The root, boiled with must, makes a rinse good for all such conditions.

HYPOGLOSSON

Some also call this plant antirrhinon, others call it areinon, and others also call it wild lychnis. It is a small shrub resembling wild myrtle, with thin leaves that are somewhat downy, and at their tip, as if little tongues, small outgrowths appear beside the leaves. It is thought that wearing it bound in the hair as an amulet is beneficial for those suffering from headaches. It is also mixed into poultices.

HYPOPHAESTON

Some also call this plant hippophaes. It grows in the same places where the true hippophaes grows, being a kind of fuller's (carding) thistle. It is a low, ground-hugging plant with heads similar [to that of the other], small thorny stems and little leaves. It bears no flower, but has a thick, soft root. Dry the leaves and head of this plant and give it as a dose in honey-water to whomever you wish; taken this way, it purges and draws out water and phlegm. It is also suitable for difficulty in breathing, for epileptic fits, and for diseases of the spleen.

translation: ...having leaves, and a third kind of mullein called lychnitis, by some called "ryallis," having more and thicker, shaggy leaves, useful for lamp-wicks. Now of the first two kinds the root is astringent, wherefore when pounded into pieces about the size of a knucklebone it is usefully given in wine as a drink. A decoction of it is also given for ruptures and spasms and bruises, and it helps those afflicted with a severe cough; it is also used as a mouthwash for toothache. The golden-flowered kind dyes the hair, and when it is applied, it draws together wounds. The leaves, boiled in water, are used for swellings of the eyes and inflammations, and as poultices; and for festering sores, mixed with honey or wine. Mixed with vinegar it heals wounds and helps those stung by scorpions. The leaves of the wild kind make a similar poultice. The leaves of the female plant, they say, when combined with dried figs, preserve meats in the same way [keep them from spoiling].

translation:
CXLIX.

TRAGORIGANON (Goat-marjoram)

It is a shrub similar to oregano or wild thyme in its leaves and twigs. In some places a stronger and broader-leaved kind is found, which some call Prasion, others call it by the name given by Aristhenes, and others call it Smyrnean or Cretan. It loosens the bowels when its decoction is drunk, for it brings down bile. Spanish varieties too, when sprinkled with vinegar, are made into a relish; taken with wine they bring on the menses. It helps also with inflammations of the lungs when taken with honey, and it is given to those who have lost their voice, and it relieves nausea and warmth of the upper abdomen. It also helps swellings when applied as a poultice mixed with barley meal.

TRAGOS, or TRAGEION, or SKORPIOS, or GARGANON

Some call it Tragion, others Tragokeros, others Skorpion, others Garganon; the Romans call it Cornulaca, others Vitouensa, others Irkoulou Dentaria; the Dacians call it Salia; the Egyptians call it Sober; the Africans call it Achchoioueim. Its leaves resemble those of the hart's-tongue fern (skolopendrion); its root is white, thin, and altogether like that of wild radish. It helps those suffering from dysentery when taken as a draught and also when boiled... it yields about ten [parts/leaves]. In autumn the leaves have the smell of a goat, from which it gets its name. It grows on headlands and cliffs.

SKANDYX                      SPARTOS                        STAPHISAGRIA

The Romans call it "erba canaria," others call it "akouklam." This too is a kind of wild chervil, somewhat bitter, edible when cooked, good for the stomach, and a diuretic. Its decoction is useful for the bladder, and it is good to drink for those with kidney and bladder troubles.

[Concerning hellebore-like properties, continued below columns:]
With considerable straining, like hellebore, but without danger. Its fruit also brings about the lower purgation, and the same rods, soaked in water, then pounded and their juice extracted, are a remedy for sciatica — about a cupful being drunk for several days. Some, having soaked them, use them as an enema for sciatica sufferers; it also brings out bloody and fermented matter.

SPARTOS — Others call it "lobon," others "lygon." It is a shrub bearing long, leafy, hard-to-break branches, with which they bind vines. It bears pods like the kidney bean, containing lentil-shaped seeds; its flower is pale yellow like the wallflower. Taking the seed-pod and the flowers steeped in honey-water, to the weight of five obols, purges from above...

[continued below, shared text block:]
Taking fifteen of its seeds... in honey-water purges by vomiting; one should walk about briskly afterward; but one must take care with the dosage.

STAPHISAGRIA — Others call it "triphyllon," others "stesion," others "staphis," others "phtheiroktonon" (lice-killer), others "phtheirion," others "apanthropon," others "polyeidos," others "pseudopathes," others "arsenope," others "arneopolemion." The Egyptians call it "ibisaoiē," the Romans "erba pedicularia," others "mioutessouda." Its leaves are like those of the wild vine, deeply cut, with upright, soft stalks. Its flower resembles that of the wild one; its fruit is in small green pods, like a triangular chickpea, thick and somewhat yellowish; inside the dark husk it has white [seeds].

cultivated parsnip

Cultivated staphylinos

CULTIVATED STAPHYLINOS (PARSNIP) · WILD

The Romans call it "pastinaca," the Africans call it "sixxam," others call it "sikkiriam," others "cultivated staphyleinos." It is edible when old; it also resembles the wild kind, though it is somewhat less effective in action.

wild parsnip

Wild staphylinos

...LINOS WILD

Some call it "keras," others "keraskomenka"; the Romans call it "carota"; others call it "pastinaca rustica"; the Egyptians call it "babiburu"; the Africans call it "sixxam." Its leaf is similar to that of hartwort, but broader and somewhat bitter. It bears a mountain stalk, rough, with an umbel resembling that of dill, from which come white flowers, purple in the middle, and somewhat saffron-colored. Its root is about the thickness of a finger, as long as a hand's breadth, fragrant, edible when boiled. Its fruit, when drunk, induces menstruation and is suitable for those with difficulty urinating, and for dropsical and pleuritic patients when taken as a drink; it is also good against the bites of wild animals. They say that those who take it beforehand are not harmed by wild beasts. It also helps conception, being diuretic, and stimulates intercourse; when applied, it expels the embryo. The leaves, pounded smooth with honey and applied, cleanse spreading (gangrenous) sores.

SPHONDYLION

Some call it dragne, others phalarion, others asterion,
others nesyris, others sphondylis, others chordanon,
others oinanthe; the Romans [call it] erbarou,
the Egyptians apher, the prophets osiris.
Its leaves are somewhat similar to those of
opopanax, broad like plane leaves; its stems are about a cubit
long, or even longer, resembling those of fennel,
with umbels in which the seed at the tip is similar
to that of seseli, double, broader and
more pale and more chaff-like; its flowers are
white or pale yellow; its root resembles that of
the radish. It grows in marshy and damp
places. Its fruit, when drunk, purges
phlegmatic matter from the belly; and when drunk
it helps those with jaundice and liver disease, and those with ailments
of the spleen, and also uterine
suffocation when fumigated, it revives those
who have fainted. Soaked in oil

and the lethargic, and checks headaches; and
spread with rue, it is applied as a plaster to herpetic sores. Its root
also is given to the jaundiced and those with liver disease; wrapped around,
and bound on, it is useful against calluses
and fistulas. The juice of its flower is good
for sweetened (discharging) ears and for ears that run with pus.

juices.

SPHONDYLION
SCOLOPENDRION, SCOLOP[...]

When eaten it promotes urination and is good for dropsical conditions.
It relieves choking and the windpipe, and soothes chronic coughs, whether eaten raw
or roasted. A decoction of it destroys lice and nits, and when drunk it benefits
the kidneys. If mixed with honey, it heals bruises and cases of alopecia (hair loss)
when applied as an ointment; for alopecia it works especially well when combined with nard ointment.
Mixed with salt and oil, it cures scrofulous swellings, and it also clears away
vitiligo, lichen-like skin conditions, and scaly patches; combined with a little
frankincense and boiled, it is used for toothaches, held in the mouth.
It is also used as a poultice for shrew-bites, together with fig leaves
and cumin. A decoction of its root, used as a sitz-bath, brings on menstruation
and fumigation with it helps sluggish bowels; it is effective against leprosy when applied directly from the plant itself.
And from wild olive oil a preparation is made, called "myt[...]",
which, when eaten, also promotes urination.

F
"Tame chicory" (seris hemeros)

153 (chapter heading)

The Egyptians call it pikridion, the Romans call it "agon," [or] "intubus agreste," others call it "kikirbita alba," others call it "amaritudo."

Others call it "kichorion," others call it "pikris agria" [wild chicory]; the Egyptians call it "agonouchi," the Romans call it "kikirbita agreste."

Of these, the wild bitter-lettuce (pikris), which is also called "kichorion," is of a certain kind, and it is broader-leaved than the cultivated garden kind, and differs from it in appearance — for there is one kind that is more like a lettuce and broad-leaved, and another that is narrow-leaved. All are bitter, and all are astringent and good for the stomach; they stop looseness of the bowels and settle the belly when eaten boiled with vinegar, and especially the wild kinds. When cooked, they restore the stomach and soothe burning sensations, especially when applied as a poultice with barley meal; and taken by themselves they are helpful for cardiac complaints. They are also useful against gout and help relieve inflammations of the eyes. Both the plant and the root, when applied as a poultice, help those stung by scorpions, and cure erysipelas when mixed with barley meal; and their juice, applied as an ointment, [is useful] for those needing cooling treatment.

SONCHUS (ROUGH)     SONCHUS (TENDER)     SESELI
                                          OF MASSILIA

The Romans know it as "cichorion"; the Romans call it "kikirbita alspra"; the Africans "gathouon nim."
There are two kinds of this plant: one is wilder and more thorny, the other more tender and edible. The stem is angular, somewhat hollow, and sometimes reddish; the leaves are divided at intervals around their edges. Their property is a moderately cooling, somewhat astringent one. Hence it is applied as a poultice for a burning or inflamed stomach. Its juice, when drunk, soothes gnawing pain of the stomach and curdles milk. Applied effectively, it helps inflammations of the anus and womb. The herb and root, applied as a poultice, help against scorpion stings.

   | The Romans know it as "cichorion"; the Romans [call it] "kikirbita molle"; the Africans "gasonim."

                                          | It is also known as "sphagnon." It has leaves resembling fennel, but thinner; it has a stem more vigorous, about a span [in height], with a double flower-head; outside it is smooth [platanos-like], bearing an elongated, angular, pungent, strong-smelling fruit; the root is long and fragrant. Its properties: the fruit and root are warming; when drunk they help strangury and [other ailments related to urination and the womb]... it helps hysterical conditions and is generally beneficial for all such complaints, whether applied as embrocation or otherwise.

It is also digestive and relieves colic, useful for other purposes as well, and against chills encountered while travelling it is mixed and warmed together with other remedies; and besides this, it is suitable for use with other ailments concerning the seat of digestion.

SESELI OF ETHIOPIA · SESELI · SCAMMONIA
OF THE PELOPONNESE ·

The Egyptians call it kynokephali.
This is the plant called Ethiopian
Seseli. It has leaves similar
to ivy, but smaller
and more elongated,
than those of the burning [plant].
It is a large shrub, about
two cubits tall, from which
grow stems a span long,
with heads like
those of dill; the seed is
black, dense like pepper,
sharper
and more fragrant
than that of the Massalian kind,
and very pleasant.
It is able to do
these same things [medicinally].

This one, which grows
in the Peloponnese,
has conical leaves,
similar but
broader and thicker,
with a stem larger
than that of the Massalian
fennel-giant; at the top
of it the fruit is
broader and
more fragrant; it has the power
to cause nausea.
It grows in
rough and
moist, shaded places.

This is the root of Scammonia,
also called Colophonia, also
Lacrydion; the Romans
call it Colophonium; it is prescribed
for the lungs; the Egyptians
call it Sanelum.
It sends up many shoots
from a single root, three cubits
or four cubits long, oily,
showing their
hairiness; and the leaves
are rough, similar to bindweed or
ivy but softer,
triangular, white when young,
rounded, hollow like
those of mallow; it has a heavy smell. The root
is long and thick, about
as thick as an arm, white, with a heavy smell, full of sap within.
The juice is collected by removing the head
of the root entirely, and
hollowing it out so that
the sap flows into the cavity, and thus from it...

PROLOGUE [illegible] [illegible]

...thicker at the top, rather like that of the lotus. There also grow from it certain hairy, fast-growing shoots. The fruit is hard, as is that of the other kind. Both kinds are astringent and cooling. They are used as a poultice for every kind of inflammation; mixed with honey, they treat mouth ulcers, tonsils, and gum disease. They are also pressed into juice for use in eye ailments. Their fruit, when green, taken as a drink helps those suffering from stones. About one drachm of the wild (land-growing) kind, taken as a drink, restores those bitten by vipers. It is also effective against deadly poisons when taken with wine. A decoction sprinkled from its leaves also kills [pests/vermin].

The Thracians who live along the river Strymon feed the green herb to their cattle, and they make a sweet and nourishing food from the fruit, using it in place of bread.

Left plant, labeled "Spartanion/Ρατάνιον"

SPARGANION (Bur-reed)
Some call it xiphidion ("little sword"). It has leaves like a little sword, with spines, and some call it "distinguished" because of the tip of its stem; it appears as if burning. Its fruit hangs from the root, and the fruit together with wine is applied to those bitten [by venomous creatures].

It grows in fields and in rocky, rough places. It has a warming and sharp power, and so a decoction of its leaves, when drunk, brings on the menses and other [discharges].

STACHYS (Spike-lavender)
Some call it stachys, others tripolion; the Romans call it trifarium. It resembles leek, but is taller, having many small leaves set at intervals, round, somewhat hairy and hard, fragrant, with a white, slender root. This differs from other roots in being whiter than those of the paliouros [Christ's thorn], under which it grows.

SKOLYMOS (Golden thistle)
Some call it ferula, others pyracantha; the Romans [call it so], the Egyptians call it "knous." It has leaves similar to those of the white thistle called embathe, darker and broader, and it has a sharp thorn around the leaves. It thrives in sunny places. When the root is taken it is similarly fragrant, and is also beneficial against a headache when applied; it is useful for difficulty urinating when drunk, and some take it for food, boiled, and it is also good for sores.

The Romans call [this plant] Beta Sylvatica. There are two kinds: the black one is more astringent to the bowels, especially when boiled, and more suited to the stomach, while the white one is more laxative. Both, because they contain something nitrous, are sharp, from which their juice cleanses the head when poured in with honey, and it helps earaches. A decoction of the roots and leaves is cleansing of dandruff and nits, and when poured over the hips it soothes them. Likewise, the leaves, applied as a plaster, cure vitiligo previously treated with nitre, and scurfy bald patches that have been scraped, and spreading sores. They also heal eruptions, burns, and erysipelas when applied as a poultice.

This is a small river-plant, a span high or larger, having leaves similar to those of pennyroyal. The leaves have very fine, smooth, divided little branches; they most resemble the leaves of wild cumin, though even finer still. Its umbel is also denser and thicker, and bears small spike-like projections above the little umbels. It has small white flowers after the manner of a bloom. It grows in fields, in rough places, and especially along roadsides. Its decoction is very good for hemorrhages, both old and fresh wounds, and for fistulas.

160.

They also call the river [plant] "Stratiotes" (Soldier); the Egyptians call it "Pibour," the priests call it "Haimadilourou" (Blood of the Crocodile). It is so named because it is accustomed to float upon the waters without roots, and lives. It has leaves similar to those of the house-leek, but larger. It has a cooling power, and when drunk it checks hemorrhages from the kidneys. It also keeps wounds from becoming inflamed, and heals erysipelas and swellings when applied as a poultice.

SESAMOIDES, THE GREAT

Some call it sesameitis, others sesameis, others wolf's-club (lykoskytalion), others white hellebore, others call it "Antikyrikon hellebore" because it is mixed into the purgatives made from white hellebore. It resembles the plant erigeron; its leaves are long, its flower white, its roots thin and ineffective, and its seed is like that of sesame. It is given... it purges the upper belly of phlegm and bile. It is administered by the measure of three fingers together with three half-obols of white hellebore, taken with melikraton (a honey-water drink).

SESAMOIDES, THE WHITE

Some call it koronion, others wild sesamion. Its stems are about a span high, bearing leaves similar to those of koronopodion, but hairier and smaller than these; at the tips of the stems are heads of a purplish hue, within which is a seed resembling that of sesame... It purges bile and phlegm when drunk... Applied as a plaster with water, its leaves [are said to help with] scrofulous swellings. It differs [from the former] and grows in rough places...

SISYMBRION

Some call it herpyllon (wild thyme), others "Aphrodite's crown"; the Romans [call it by another name]... It is a shrub-like plant [growing in dry places?]... it grows in barren ground... [the rest of this column is too faded to read with confidence].

SISYMBRION, ANOTHER KIND

[This column is largely illegible due to fading, but based on the surviving fragments it continues the description of a second type of sisymbrium, noting its appearance, where it grows, and its medicinal uses — likely similar digestive and soothing properties as related mint-family herbs, consistent with the entries of Dioscorides' De Materia Medica.]

CLXII.

WILD CELERY                      ANOTHER
                                   WILD CELERY

Also called batrachion, also called "the joker" (gelotopoios), also
called "the drunken one" (methyousa), also called sardonion, also called ambeuston;
also called hyoselinon, also called hipposelinon by the Egyptians;
the Romans call it "methyou"; also called apiumonor, also apiourion;
also called aurimetellus; in Tuscan, apiouraninou.

There are several species of these plants, with a sharp and
ulcer-inducing property. One of them has dry leaves,
similar but broader and somewhat whitish,
oily, with a pale yellow flower — sometimes also purple, depending on the
variations of locality in Sardinia — a rather thick stem, with a white,
bitter root that sends out shoots like those of the olive. It grows near
waters; there is also another kind, more snow-white, with longer, hollow,
jointed stems, having more incisions in its leaves than the first.
The most potent is the one growing in Sardinia, which indeed is
called "wild celery" and also "three-eyed" (trioph­thalma); it is
small, foul-smelling, golden in flower, and grape-like in clusters,
with milky-white blossoms. All these have similar power when applied
as a poultice: they are corrosive and cauterizing, causing pain
when used, and they remove discolorations from the skin; they also
remove blemishes, warts, and skin growths, as well as leprous spots,
when mixed in and applied evenly; and in this way they also
dissolve (soften) baths when lukewarm, being a remedy; they are also
good against toothache when used appropriately, relieving
it when rubbed on.

Also called phrynion, also
batrachion by the Romans;
"apius flavus" (yellow celery).

PHYTEUMA
The Romans call it "aploumerou." It has leaves similar to the small bird-wort (astroulion), but smaller, and a fruit full of... a long, double root spreading on the surface. Some have written that it is useful for a love-charm.

PHALERION
It has thin stalks with many joints, from slender roots, like reeds, most similar in habit to spelt (zea), but more slender and sweet to the taste, and leaves similar to those of spelt. The seed is about the size of millet, white, and oblong. The plant, when pounded and its juice strained in water, has the property of relieving pains of the bladder; and a spoonful of the seed drunk with water produces the same effect.

PHOINIX
Some call it "rous," others "anchynon," others "phoinikopteros," others "rousostachys," the Romans call it "ostham," the Egyptians "palodou" or "pinouda," or "donou." Its leaves are similar to those of barley, but shorter and narrower, with an ear... growing in a circle around the root to about six finger-widths, and bearing up to eight ears. It grows in the fields and on rooftops. It has the property, when drunk with astringent wine, of stopping diarrhea and hemorrhage from the womb, and checking any excessive flow. Some say that it is also a kind of rush, and that when bound with palm-root it is worn as an amulet.

PHALANGION
It is also called phalangitis; some also
call this one leukakantha ("white-thorn").
It has branches, two or three or more,
standing apart from one another, with white
flowers altogether like those of a lily in shape.
The seed is thick and black, like
that of the lentil, but somewhat finer...
mostly... the root is slender...
green, together with it being loosened...
from the earth afterward they come together.
It grows on hilly ground.
Its leaves, seed,
and flower, when drunk
with wine, help against the bites of spiders [phalangia]
and scorpions,
and it also relieves colic.

LENTIL (Phakos)
The Romans call it "lens,"
"lenticula." When eaten
continually it dulls the eyesight,
is hard to digest, bad for the stomach,
causes flatulence of the stomach
and intestines and bowels.
It is softening when
boiled; it differs [in effect]
from the unhulled kind, and if nothing
is removed in the cooking, it is black[ish].
It has an astringent power,
hence it benefits an empty stomach
when its hull has been removed and it is boiled
carefully; and if the first
water in which it was boiled is poured off,
the broth has a loosening effect
on the bowels. It is also useful
for sinewy parts and for hemorrhage, and for
the head particularly; its proper effect is completed thereby...

LENTIL OF THE MARSHES / "FAKOS EPI TON PELMATON" (Duckweed)
It is also called epipteron, also
hyperalis, also ikeos,
found in Macedonia;
it is found floating on
still waters, resembling moss or lentil
in appearance, cooling in nature.
Hence it is suitable for all inflammations
and erysipelas
and for gout, being applied
as a plaster...
it also helps joints when bound on,
and is good for [bruises/wounds]...

[General closing note, likely about mixtures:]
...mixed together with endive, or plantain,
or black beet, or myrtle, or pomegranate rind, or roses,
or quince, or pear, or oak-galls, or acorn cups — these slip away (dissolve)
after boiling, poured off from the vinegar-mixture.

translation:
CLXV.

PHASIOLOS (bean)
"fasiolas"
It produces windy, gaseous vapors
of a generative kind,
it is hard to digest.
When boiled while still green
and eaten,
it softens the bowels,
and furthermore it is a
suitable emetic.

PHYLLITIS
"fillus"
Also known as Phyllis, also
called Acaulon, also called Lapathon
Agrion by some.
Its leaves resemble anise,
more elongated than dock,
naturally well-formed, firm,
rounded, smooth within,
and on the underside
having thin markings
like little worms.
It grows in shady places
and in gardens. Its taste
is somewhat astringent. It
bears neither stalk nor
fruit nor flower.
Its leaves, drunk with wine,
counter the bites
of crawling creatures. For
quadrupeds, when a measured
dose of its juice is given, it helps
those bitten; it is also good
against dysentery and diarrhea.

PHYLLON
"fillon"
Also known as Eleophyllon, and also
called Bryonia by some. It grows
on rocks, bearing what is called
"elyton," like a kind of moss (bryon),
having leaves greener than
olive leaves, a white stalk, and
fruit larger than that of the poppy.
The "arsogonon" variety is in every way
similar to the aforementioned,
but differs in its fruit; for it has
flowers like those of the narthex (fennel-giant),
not clustered in grape-like bunches.
It is called "arsenogonon"
because it is said to cause the birth of males,
while the "thelygonon" causes females.
Krateuas has written
about these matters, but it seems to me
that such claims go beyond
what can be properly verified by inquiry.
