Plant labels: "Jupiter's beard" root (Latin gloss), "stirobote," "aglaria," "chrysotomon," "chrysanthon, selinon."

Chapter headings: CHRYSOCOME · CHRYSOGONON · CHRYSANTHON, also called ELICHRYSOS

On Chrysocome:
The plant called Chryseitis is also known as Chrysathemon, also as Amaranthos, also as Diospyron; the Romans call it Jovis barba (Jupiter's beard), the Africans call it Doubath. It is a small shrub having a tuft of hair-like, cluster-shaped growths similar to a sprout of flax. Its root is shaggy, and when tasted it has a flying, hellebore-like quality, not winged like cypress, producing a sweet, somewhat astringent taste. It grows in shady and rocky places. It has a warming and astringent power, and is suitable for liver and lung ailments, when taken with hydromel (honey-water); it also helps as a cleansing agent for the uterus.

On Chrysogonon:
It is also known as Chrysospermon, also as Lapin, also as Linon, also as Origanon, also as Arkophallon; the Romans call it Agriaria. Its leaves resemble those of the oak, and the shrub is dense. Its flower, found all around, is used in making garlands. Its root is similar in shape, rounded, growing strongly within... it helps externally when applied, being effective, soothed with vinegar and ground fine, and applied to shrew-bites.

On Chrysanthon, also called Elichryson:
This too is called Amaranton, as it is used to crown the gods as well. It has a straight, solid stem, with narrow leaves, somewhat resembling the foliage of southernwood, round and shield-shaped, golden-bright, rounded, like clusters. Its root is thin, growing in rough and ravine-like places. Its foliage, when mixed with wine, helps against difficulty urinating, snake bites, sciatica, and uterine issues, also bringing on menstruation, and dissolves clots of blood in the bladder — drunk with wine or honey-wine. It also helps with sciatica and chronic catarrh when given fasting in wine. [It is] mixed with white... and preserved with garments to keep moths away most effectively.

translation:
CLXVII. 167

CHRYSANTHEMON
OR CHALKAS

Some call it chrysanthemis, others chalkitis, others chalkanthon, others chalkanthaimon, others call it buphthalmon; the Romans call it acantha, the Thuscans garouleon, the Africans chourzeta. It is a somewhat delicate plant, shrub-like, with smooth stems rising up, and leaves finely divided, and flowers of a golden color shining strongly, round like eyes — hence it has been so named. It grows around cities; its stalks are eaten as a vegetable. Its flowers, crushed and mixed with wax ointment, are said to disperse fatty swellings. For jaundiced patients it also produces a good complexion for a time, when applied after the long exertion of bathing.

CHONDROS

Some call it dikokkon, others call it zea; the Romans call it far. Chondros is made from the so-called "two-grained" zea; it is the most nourishing of foods, like rice, and binding to the bowels, though less easy on the stomach when fresh. When ground fine and applied, it removes leprous conditions of the nails, and it begins to heal incipient aigilops (a kind of eye ulcer) when used as an enema in a decoction. A decoction of it is also suitable to use for the pain of dysentery.

CHONDRILE

Some also call this kichorion (chicory), others call it seris. Its leaves, stem, and flowers resemble chicory, whence some call it "wild seris." The whole plant is more slender. Around its small stalks there forms a gum-like substance, resembling rows of grains the size of a bean, which, when combined with myrrh in a linen cloth about the size of an olive, induces menstruation. The herb itself, when pounded, is preserved in the form of lozenges, and is used after being mixed with honey. These, when dissolved and combined with soda (nitron), scour away stones. The gum also serves to glue hair back on, and the fresh root does the same, when the hair is dipped into it.

[Column 2 — on Psyllium]
It is also known as "katafysis," also "kynokephalion," also "krystallion," also "kynomyia," also "psylaeris," also "Sikeliotikon" by the Sicilians, commonly called by the Romans "silvaticum," also "herba pulicaris" by the Africans, "uargugum." Its leaf resembles that of coronopus, but hairy and longer; the branches are about a span long, and the whole plant is grass-like. Its foliage begins from the middle of the stem; the heads, two or three, are twisted together at the tip, and the seed resembles fleas — black and hard. It grows in cultivated fields.

It has a cooling property and is beneficial, when made into a plaster, for arthritis, swollen glands (parotids), tumors, inflammations, spasms, and headache (mixed with rose oil and vinegar-water); also for intestinal hernias in children and for protruding navels, when applied as a poultice. One should steep a generous amount — about an oxybaphon's worth — in two kotylai of water, and drink it mild throughout; it cools sufficiently.

[Column 3 — on Pseudobounion]
It is a shrub, growing densely in Crete, having leaves like... similar to..., with about four branches growing from it. Taken with water it is said to cure colic, strangury, and pains of the side (pleurisy); it also helps with scrofulous swellings... when taken warm with wine.

CHAMAIDAPHNE                CHAMAISYKE                CHAMAIMELON

Those in Alexandria call this plant [Chamaidaphne]; others call it daphneitis, the Egyptians "hydragogos," the Romans "lauriola" ["lyriphola"], others "lalagon," and still others "ousouben." It sends up only shoots, straight and very slender, with leaves like those of the bay (laurel), but much smoother and smaller, bearing a round, reddish fruit growing upon the leaves. Its leaves, when applied as a poultice, help afflictions of the head and stomach in cases of burning fevers. Taken in wine, they check [certain] fluxes. Its juice, mixed with honey, and applied as a salve, helps the eyes; sprinkled on, it does the same thing when so applied.

[Chamaisyke:] Some call this plant "syke," others "mekon," the Egyptians call it "aphyis," others "klosis," others "anisis," and "tetradaktylos," because it lies spread upon the ground. It bears leaves like lentil, flat, similar to purslane; its fruit is small, round in the leaves; it has a flower like that of the fig (syke); its root is of no use. Its properties are useful against the stings of scorpions and the beginnings of a cataract-like dimming of vision; applied as an ointment it is dissolving; it is given to drink for those suffering from dry [ailments/coughs].

translation: [Its leaves] enclosing it, and on the outside there lies around it a round-shaped white, pale, or purple (flower), about the size of a rue leaf. It grows in rough places and alongside roads, and is gathered in spring. The root, the herb, and the flowers all have a heating property. When drunk, and when used as a sitz-bath, they bring on the menses, [expel] the embryo and stones, and promote urination. They are also given to drink for flatulence and colic; they cleanse those with jaundice and are used as a poultice. Their decoctions are taken for bladder trouble. More effective among the varieties for individual purposes is the purple-flowered kind, which common people consider larger, properly called the "eranthemon" (ground-flower). The hyacinth-colored kind is less effective for this purpose, as is the golden-flowered kind (chrysanthemum). They are therapeutically applied when arranged [as poultices] and when chewed; some people use them mixed with ointment, grinding them with oil for the treatment of periodic (recurring) fevers. The leaves and flowers of each kind are stored, being pounded and made up into small lozenges together with the dried root, to be given whenever need demands. The taste of the herb's one part is sweet, while the other, sharper part is pungent; it should be drunk mixed with wine and honey.

CHAMAELEON WHITE·

Some call it "golden sceptre," others "ixia." The Romans call it "cardos ularinos," others "pine-cardos," others "lacte-cardos." The Egyptians call it "ephonr," others call it "boiled-possessing ixia," naming it so because in certain places it is found growing near the roots of mistletoe, and the women use it in place of mastic gum. It has leaves similar to the milk-thistle or the golden thistle, but thicker and sharper than the black kind. It has no stem, but sends up from the middle a spine resembling that of the sea-artichoke (cynara); its flowers are purplish, like hairs, and its fruit resembles that of safflower. Its root, in rich soil, is thick, but in mountainous regions thinner; it is white, aromatic, has a heavy smell, and is sweet. When drunk, it expels broad tapeworms — a handful's weight taken with wine, [along] with a decoction of dried oregano; and it is suitable, taken as a decoction, also to induce sweating, for it makes thin; it is given in a dose of one "holke" with wine, [to help] those boiled for it, and also for difficulty urinating. Drunk with wine it also serves as an antidote against venomous bites; it kills dogs as well, when mixed with [other things] and applied as described.

CHAMAIAKTE (also called "chalus")

CHAMAIAKTE: Some call it heleoakte, others wild akte (elder), others the Euboean [elder]; the Romans call it ebulum, the Gauls dukone, the Dacians olma. It sends up a square, many-jointed stem, with leaves like those of the elder, woolly, and all around similar, heavy-smelling, smaller in a circle, and the long elder — both in its flower and in its fruit — is similar; it has a pith the thickness of a reed. Its property is drying and astringent, inducing sleep. The leaves, when boiled, purge phlegm and bile as a potherb does; the tender shoots, when taken in food, do the same; and its root, boiled in wine and given, dissolves dropsy; and boiled with water it cleanses the womb's obstructions, opens them, and sets right the conditions around it; the fruit does the same as the leaf. Mixed with other leaves it is used as a poultice against swellings, and when rubbed on, it also soothes the hair of the lower parts. Mixed with barley meal it is suitable as a plaster for wounds that need to be drawn together, and for prolapses; it is also applied with goat fat as a poultice.

CHAMAIKISSOS (Ground Ivy)

CHAMAIKISSOS: Some call it chamai[...]en, kissos akar[...], stephanos; the Romans call it ede[ra?]. Its leaves resemble [ivy], but are smaller [...] in a circlet [...] with white flowers [...] smaller [...] in taste. Its root is slender and useful. It grows in cultivated and fallow ground, and is good for sciatica sufferers: a cyathos [dose] taken with three parts water for forty days cleanses [...] applied for [...] days.
